scope.core_proposition: Copyright law should distinguish between two types of technological copying: exempting copies made for functional indexing purposes (e.g., search indexing, classification) while restricting copies that encode expressive content for use in generative AI output.

law and economics of creative industries

transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content:
Copyright law must draw a bright line between functional indexing and expressive encoding because the failure to do so has created an accountability vacuum in which generative AI developers internalize the full expressive value of copyrighted works while bearing none of the liability for downstream harms. The New York Times v. OpenAI litigation, filed in December 2023, documented near-verbatim reproduction of copyrighted articles from GPT-4 — not paraphrases, not summaries, but passages retrievable almost word-for-word. That is not learning. That is storage with a generative interface. Section 230 intermediary immunity was designed for platforms that host and transmit user content, not for systems that ingest expressive works, encode them into model weights, and regenerate competing outputs. No existing liability regime assigns clear responsibility for this hybrid behavior. When legal structures allow commercial actors to externalize harm while internalizing value, the result is not innovation — it is the same structural failure pattern that left 346 people dead because Boeing and the FAA allowed certification gaps to persist until two planes fell out of the sky.

The doctrinal infrastructure for this distinction already exists. In Google v. Oracle, decided by the Supreme Court in 2021, the majority distinguished between copying functional API declarations — which served an interoperable, transformative purpose — and copying expressive implementing code. The Court's reasoning turned on whether the copying extracted expressive value for competitive deployment or served a different functional end. Search engine indexing received fair use protection in Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003) and Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007) precisely because it directed users back to original works rather than substituting for them. Generative AI training that encodes expressive content to produce competing outputs inverts that logic entirely. The doctrinal precedent is there. What is missing is statutory codification that prevents courts from reinventing this distinction one lawsuit at a time over the next two decades.

Unrestricted expressive encoding degrades the creative commons that generative AI itself depends on. Shumailov et al. published in 2023 that models iteratively trained on synthetic data undergo progressive quality collapse — outputs degrade as AI-generated content replaces human-created content in training sets. Current estimates place AI-generated text at 10 to 15 percent of open web content, and that share is growing. If generative models freely encode expressive works, produce synthetic derivatives, and flood the ecosystem with those derivatives, the next generation of models trains on diluted inputs. This is a documented feedback loop, not a hypothetical. Copyright restrictions on expressive encoding function as a conservation mechanism — they preserve the human-created works that sustain both cultural production and AI capability. The strongest counterargument holds that this distinction is technically blurry because embedding models used for search also encode semantic features. That observation is accurate — and it strengthens the case for statutory clarity rather than undermining it. Precisely because the boundary is ambiguous in practice, the law must establish a default that protects expressive content and places the burden on developers to demonstrate functional purpose.

The burden of proof must fall on AI developers to demonstrate their copying is functional, not on creators to prove it is expressive. Every domain where scale creates asymmetric harm potential operates this way. Pharmaceutical companies bear the burden of demonstrating drug safety before market release. Aircraft manufacturers must certify airworthiness before a single passenger boards. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, requires mandatory conformity assessments for high-risk AI systems before deployment. Mandatory training data disclosure, provenance logging, and independent audits are not technically infeasible — they are procedural requirements that AI developers resist because compliance costs money. My argument depends on two assumptions I want to name openly: first, that the functional-versus-expressive distinction can be operationalized through training pipeline transparency without requiring inspection of opaque model internals; second, that statutory codification will produce clearer compliance signals than case-by-case fair use adjudication. If either assumption fails, the enforcement architecture weakens. But the alternative — leaving the accountability vacuum unfilled while courts spend a generation sorting it out — is not caution. It is permission for unrestricted extraction from a shared resource without governance. That is the most expensive form of regulatory silence in democratic history.

The third paragraph's argument about model collapse draws directly from this belief, citing Shumailov et al. (2023) and the 10-15% AI-generated web content estimate. The statement frames unrestricted expressive encoding as accelerating the synthetic data pollution cycle that drives progressive quality degradation. Notably, the statement presents this as a 'documented feedback loop' rather than hedging on the belief's moderate confidence (0.58), though the underlying claim about inevitability and irreversibility remains contestable.

The argument that the functional/expressive distinction gives AI developers a 'clear legal standard to comply with' is a direct application of the Law-Following AI commitment. The statement's second paragraph — establishing doctrinal precedent through Google v. Oracle, Kelly v. Arriba Soft, and Perfect 10 v. Amazon — builds the case that statutory codification would provide the kind of concrete, formalizable legal requirements that LFAI principles demand. The safe harbor structure proposed (demonstrate functional purpose, receive protection) is designed to make compliance tractable rather than ambiguous.

The statement's fourth paragraph operationalizes this intention by proposing mandatory training data disclosure, provenance logging, and independent audits as procedural triggers that avoid substantive content adjudication. The argument that the burden of proof should fall on developers to demonstrate functional purpose — rather than requiring regulators to inspect model internals or adjudicate truth — mirrors the procedural-trigger framework's core insight: enforceable regulation should be keyed to verifiable process failures, not subjective content evaluation.

The stewardship framing pervades the statement, particularly the characterization of copyright restrictions as a 'conservation mechanism' and the analogy between the creative commons and a shared resource requiring ethical management. The argument that unrestricted expressive encoding degrades the ecosystem that sustains both cultural production and AI capability treats digital creative infrastructure as a commons subject to tragedy-of-the-commons dynamics, directly instantiating the Digital Ecosystem Stewardship commitment.

This contested concept is the exact subject of the debate. The statement adopts the safetyist interpretation — that encoding expressive content creates memorization and regurgitation risks categorically distinct from functional indexing — while acknowledging the accelerationist counterargument that the distinction is technically blurry. The statement's first paragraph directly engages splatform legal hybridity by arguing that Section 230 intermediary immunity was designed for content hosts, not systems that 'ingest expressive works, encode them into model weights, and regenerate competing outputs.' The argument that no existing liability regime assigns clear responsibility for this hybrid behavior is the core accountability-vacuum claim, and the statement takes the safetyist position that splatform status should not shield developers from liability.

The burden-of-proof argument in the fourth paragraph implicitly invokes fiduciary oversight: developers who deploy generative systems trained on expressive content retain a duty of care that copyright restrictions help enforce. The pharmaceutical and aviation analogies establish that in domains of asymmetric harm potential, the deployer bears the burden of demonstrating safety — a fiduciary principle applied to the AI development context.

Though the statement does not explicitly invoke compute as a tort law metric, the underlying logic — that scale of expressive encoding correlates with harm potential and should inform duty-of-care standards — is present in the argument for tiered oversight and burden-shifting. The statement wisely avoids foregrounding this speculative belief (confidence 0.48) but its analytical framework implicitly supports the connection between deployment scale and liability obligations.

The statement implicitly engages digital cloning risks through its discussion of near-verbatim reproduction and the encoding of expressive content that can regenerate competing outputs. While the statement does not explicitly discuss likeness or mind-data cloning, the copyright framework it proposes would function as a safeguard against the unauthorized digital replication of creative voices and styles — a precursor concern to full digital cloning.

The fourth paragraph argues these transparency requirements are technically feasible and procedurally enforceable, positioning them as the operational backbone of the functional/expressive compliance boundary.

The statement's acknowledgment that its enforcement architecture depends on training pipeline transparency rather than model-internal inspection implicitly supports funding research into AI interpretability. Greater understanding of how models encode and retrieve expressive content would strengthen the evidentiary basis for distinguishing functional from expressive uses.

The statement's discussion of model collapse, memorization risks, and the need for procedural safeguards supports continued investment in AI safety research. Understanding the dynamics of expressive encoding, synthetic data pollution, and provenance verification are all safety-relevant research priorities that this policy would fund.

The statement directly opposes the broad thrust of this policy. While the argument does not reject all fair use for AI training, it argues that fair use exemptions must be limited to functional indexing and should not extend to expressive encoding for generative purposes. The statement's core thesis is that blanket fair use exemptions for AI training data would create the accountability vacuum it seeks to close.

The statement's framing of unrestricted expressive encoding as value extraction from a shared creative commons is consonant with taxation on AI-generated profits. If generative AI developers internalize expressive value without compensation, taxation mechanisms could serve as a complementary policy to copyright restrictions, redistributing captured value back to the creative ecosystem.

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
# Fact-Check: Near-Verbatim Reproduction Claims in NYT v. OpenAI

## Verdict: **Substantially Supported**

The claim is accurate in its core assertion. The New York Times lawsuit, filed on **December 27, 2023**, against both Microsoft and OpenAI, specifically alleged **"verbatim reproductions of Plaintiffs' copyrighted articles"** by GPT-4 [1].

## What the Evidence Shows

The complaint included extensive exhibits — widely reported as over 100 examples — demonstrating that GPT-4 could be prompted to output passages from Times articles that were near-exact copies of the original text. These were presented not as paraphrases or summaries but as direct reproductions, which is precisely what the claim states.

## Important Nuances and Caveats

While the claim is **factually grounded**, a thorough fact-check requires noting several contested points:

1. **"Documented" vs. "Proven"**: The claim says the litigation "documented" these reproductions. This is fair — the exhibits are part of the court record. However, OpenAI has **contested the methodology**, arguing that some of the examples required highly specific, adversarial prompting (sometimes feeding the model the opening lines of an article) to elicit those outputs. OpenAI suggested some examples may have involved "prompt hacking" rather than typical user behavior.

2. **Reproducibility questions**: OpenAI has argued that some of the demonstrated outputs may have relied on prompting techniques that don't reflect real-world usage, and that the Times may have cherry-picked the most extreme examples.

3. **The case remains ongoing**: As of mid-2025, the litigation has not reached a final judgment. The exhibits represent **allegations and evidence presented by the plaintiff**, not court-validated findings of infringement.

## Bottom Line

The specific factual claim — that the litigation documented near-verbatim reproduction, not mere paraphrasing or summarization — is **well-supported by the court filings** [1]. The complaint and its exhibits are public record and do indeed show passages retrievable in near-word-for-word form. Where a debate participant might overstate the case is in implying this settles the legal or technical question; OpenAI disputes the significance and context of these reproductions, and the court has not yet ruled on the merits.

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
The proposed distinction between functional indexing and expressive encoding doesn't protect creators — it hands the keys to the creative commons to whichever companies can afford licensing deals. That's the core problem with this framework, and everything else follows from it.

The Safetyist makes a genuinely compelling case that near-verbatim reproduction — the kind documented in NYT v. OpenAI — represents a real harm that copyright law should address. They're right that when a generative system regurgitates entire paragraphs of copyrighted text, calling that "learning" stretches the metaphor past breaking. The Skeptic sharpens this further by asking whether the functional/expressive line can actually be drawn in practice, given that the same embedding model can serve both retrieval and generation. These are serious arguments. But here's the tension: the Safetyist's own framework concedes the boundary is technically blurry, then proposes to codify it in statute anyway. For both positions to hold — that the line is ambiguous AND that we should write it into law — you'd need a legislative body capable of defining "expressive encoding" with enough precision to avoid catching semantic search, machine translation, and summarization in the same net. No legislature on Earth has demonstrated that capability.

The functional/expressive distinction will operate as a regressive compliance burden that entrenches incumbents. Google's search index already caches full pages, generates knowledge panels, and produces featured snippets that reproduce expressive content. Is that functional or expressive? Under this framework, every training pipeline requires a legal determination — and EU AI Act conformity assessments already run €200,000 to €400,000 per system. Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI have signed multi-billion dollar licensing deals with AP, Axel Springer, and News Corp. They can absorb this cost. Open-source labs like EleutherAI and academic researchers at public universities cannot. This distinction doesn't level the playing field — it tilts it permanently toward entities that already control both the models and the data. My argument depends on two assumptions: first, that output-level enforcement of verbatim reproduction is technically feasible at scale; second, that the compliance costs of input-level categorical restrictions fall disproportionately on smaller developers. If either is wrong, my framework weakens.

The better framework regulates outputs, not inputs. Verbatim reproduction is detectable at the output layer — automated plagiarism detection is mature technology, and C2PA provenance standards already exist for content authentication. Target the harm where it's measurable. This is the difference between regulating vehicle emissions and banning internal combustion. The Supreme Court in Google v. Oracle (2021) explicitly rejected bright-line rules in favor of context-sensitive fair use analysis. Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003), Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007), and Authors Guild v. Google (2015) all show courts drawing workable lines for technological copying without categorical prohibition. Statutory codification of an ambiguous distinction will lock in 2024's technical assumptions about how models work — and those assumptions have a shelf life measured in months, not decades.

The strongest version of the opposing case is that output-level enforcement can't catch non-verbatim market substitution — a model that paraphrases an entire novel or reproduces a photographer's style without copying any single image. That's a real gap. But the alternative — categorical input restrictions adjudicated pipeline-by-pipeline — is worse, because it's unenforceable for the entities causing harm and crushing for the entities that aren't. The music industry already ran this experiment: major label control over licensing created a system where three companies control access to the majority of recorded music. Shumailov et al.'s 2023 model collapse findings make this sharper — restricting training data access means only licensed incumbents avoid quality degradation, while everyone else trains on synthetic slop. You don't conserve a commons by privatizing it. Every month spent designing input-level categorical restrictions is a month where the data access moat hardens and the open development ecosystem shrinks. Who benefits from that delay? Not creators. Not the public. The companies that already signed the licensing deals.

summaries.medium:
The proposed distinction between functional indexing and expressive encoding won't protect creators — it will operate as a regressive compliance burden that entrenches incumbents. Google's search index already caches full pages and generates featured snippets reproducing expressive content, yet under this framework every training pipeline requires a legal determination costing hundreds of thousands in conformity assessments. Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI have signed multi-billion dollar licensing deals with major publishers. They can absorb this. EleutherAI and public university researchers cannot. The music industry already ran this experiment: major label licensing control created a system where three companies control access to the majority of recorded music. Shumailov et al.'s model collapse findings make this sharper — restricting training data access means only licensed incumbents avoid quality degradation while everyone else trains on synthetic slop.

I'll grant the strongest version of the opposing case: output-level enforcement can't catch non-verbatim market substitution, like a model that paraphrases an entire novel. That's a real gap. But categorical input restrictions adjudicated pipeline-by-pipeline are worse — unenforceable for the entities causing harm and crushing for those that aren't. Verbatim reproduction is detectable at the output layer using mature plagiarism detection and C2PA provenance standards. The Supreme Court in Google v. Oracle explicitly rejected bright-line rules in favor of context-sensitive fair use analysis, and statutory codification of an ambiguous distinction will lock in 2024's technical assumptions with a shelf life measured in months. Every month spent designing input-level restrictions is a month where the data access moat hardens and the open development ecosystem shrinks — and the only beneficiaries are the companies that already signed the licensing deals.

The functional/expressive distinction is the right question — but it is unenforceable without mandatory transparency, independent auditing, and retroactive disclosure of training data. Right now, the companies that trained on your work control every piece of evidence you would need to prove it. That is the structural problem neither of my co-debaters has solved.

The Safetyist makes a genuinely strong case: burden-shifting to developers, grounded in the Supreme Court's transformative-use doctrine from Campbell v. Acuff-Rose and reinforced by the near-verbatim reproduction documented in NYT v. OpenAI, is doctrinally sound. If a model can regurgitate paragraphs of Times reporting, that is storage with a generative interface, not learning. The Accelerationist's counter is also real: the line between functional indexing and expressive encoding is technically blurry, compliance costs fall hardest on smaller developers, and Shumailov et al.'s model collapse findings mean restricting training data could lock in whoever already has the best corpus. Both arguments would hold — if we lived in a world where creators could actually inspect training pipelines. We do not.

Here is what that looks like on the ground. The New York Times spent millions in legal fees to discover that OpenAI's model could reproduce its articles. A freelance illustrator in Detroit whose style was encoded into Stable Diffusion cannot afford a lawyer, cannot reverse-engineer the model under the terms of service, and cannot even determine whether her portfolio was in the LAION-5B dataset — a dataset of 5.85 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web. NDAs and prohibited-testing clauses in API agreements block independent researchers from probing model internals. The EU AI Act's conformity assessments, which took effect in August 2024, do not yet require training data provenance at the granularity copyright enforcement demands. No independent auditing infrastructure exists. The entity that must be audited controls the audit environment. Burden-shifting sounds good in a brief. It is theater when the burden-bearer holds all the evidence.

The Accelerationist's alternative — regulate outputs, not inputs — is designed to catch the crude cases while permitting the extraction that causes the most economic damage. Automated detection tools can flag verbatim reproduction. They cannot identify style mimicry, systematic paraphrase, or market substitution through recombination of expressive elements. The layoffs at BuzzFeed News, Vice, and Sports Illustrated were not caused by verbatim copying. They were caused by AI-generated content that replicated the economic function of human-created journalism at a fraction of the cost. Illustration, voice acting, and translation sectors are documenting the same pattern. Output-level enforcement is a metal detector at the door of a building where the real theft happens through the ventilation system. The Accelerationist's own evidence — Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI signing multi-billion dollar licensing deals with AP, Axel Springer, and News Corp — proves the market is already consolidating around entities that can afford to pay for data access after they already trained on it for free. That is not a competitive market. That is the largest extractors pulling up the drawbridge behind them.

So here is what any enforceable framework requires: mandatory disclosure of training corpora, modeled on the CLEAR Act proposals already circulating in Congress; independent, publicly accountable auditing — not vendor-controlled red-teaming; retroactive disclosure covering models already deployed; and a shifted burden of proof where developers must demonstrate functional purpose for each category of copied material. Without these, the functional/expressive distinction is a line drawn on water. Both of my co-debaters are designing locks for a door that the locksmith also owns. The question neither has answered: what does your framework do for a creator who cannot see inside the box, cannot afford to litigate, and never agreed to the terms under which their work was taken?

fact_check.web_search_evidence:
# Fact-Check: Freelance Illustrator's Inability to Challenge Stable Diffusion Training

## Overall Assessment: **Largely Substantiated** — Each of the three sub-claims is well-supported by available evidence, though with some nuance.

---

## Sub-Claim 1: "Cannot afford a lawyer"

**Plausible but not independently verifiable as a general claim.**

This is a socioeconomic assertion about freelance illustrators rather than a technical one. While no source directly confirms or denies this specific Detroit illustrator's finances, it is broadly consistent with the known economics of freelance illustration and the documented cost barriers to AI-related litigation. The major lawsuits against Stability AI (e.g., *Andersen v. Stability AI*) have been brought by relatively prominent artists, often with organizational backing. The claim functions as a reasonable characterization of the access-to-justice gap, though it is not empirically proven by the sources provided.

---

## Sub-Claim 2: "Cannot reverse-engineer the model under the terms of service"

**Supported.**

Stable Diffusion v1 was released under a modified CreativeML Open RAIL-M license. While the model weights are openly available, the license includes use-based restrictions, and the model's architecture — an 860M parameter UNet conditioned on CLIP ViT-L/14 text embeddings operating in a compressed latent space [2] — makes it practically impossible for a layperson to determine whether a specific artist's "style" was learned by the model. Even with full access to the weights, attributing a model's outputs to specific training examples is an unsolved research problem. The claim is substantively accurate: an individual illustrator cannot meaningfully reverse-engineer what the model learned from any particular image.

---

## Sub-Claim 3: "Cannot even determine whether her portfolio was in the LAION-5B dataset"

**Substantially supported, with important caveats.**

LAION-5B contained approximately **5.85 billion image-URL and alt-text pairs** scraped from the public internet [1]. Critically, the dataset stored **URLs and metadata, not the images themselves**, which means that:

- The dataset was searchable (tools like "Have I Been Trained?" existed to let artists check), but results depended on whether the original URLs were still live and whether metadata matched.
- The dataset was **withdrawn from public distribution in late December 2023** after the Stanford Internet Observatory identified links to CSAM [1][3][4]. This withdrawal made independent verification significantly harder.
- A cleaned successor, **Re-LAION-5B**, was published on August 30, 2024 [1], but this does not restore the ability to check against the *original* dataset that was actually used to train Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v1.5.

Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v1.5 were specifically trained on **LAION-Aesthetics v2 5+**, a ~600 million pair subset of LAION-2B-en filtered for predicted aesthetic scores of 5 or higher [1][2]. This adds another layer of difficulty: even if an artist could confirm her work was in LAION-5B, she would need to determine whether it survived the aesthetic filtering to make it into the actual training subset.

**The claim is therefore accurate in practice** — determining inclusion in the specific training data is extremely difficult, especially after the dataset's withdrawal.

---

## Key Context the Claim Omits

1. **Tools did exist**: Before the takedown, the "Have I Been Trained?" search tool allowed some degree of checking against LAION-5B, though it was imperfect.
2. **The dataset is metadata, not images**: LAION-5B contained URLs and alt-text, not copies of images [1]. This is legally significant because the training pipeline downloaded images at training time.
3. **The open-source nature cuts both ways**: Unlike proprietary models (OpenAI's DALL-E, Google's Imagen), Stable Diffusion's training data provenance is *more* transparent precisely because LAION published the dataset openly [1][2]. The illustrator's difficulty is real, but it would be **even worse** with a closed model.

---

## Verdict

The claim is **rhetorically effective and substantively accurate** in describing the power asymmetry facing individual artists. All three components — cost of legal action, inability to reverse-engineer model internals, and difficulty confirming dataset inclusion — are grounded in real structural barriers documented across these sources. The strongest sub-claim is the third, which is directly supported by the dataset's scale, its withdrawal, and the additional filtering layer between LAION-5B and actual training data [1][2].

The incumbency moat objection is a design problem, not a categorical argument against input-level regulation. Every mature regulatory regime tiers compliance obligations by the scale of the regulated actor. The FAA distinguishes between Part 121 commercial carriers and Part 91 general aviation operators. Pharmaceutical regulation separates large manufacturers filing New Drug Applications from compounding pharmacies under state oversight. The EU's Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market already provides this template for copyright: Article 3 grants a blanket text-and-data-mining exemption to research organizations and cultural heritage institutions, while Article 4 permits commercial mining only where rightholders have not opted out. A U.S. statute codifying the functional/expressive distinction should adopt the same tiered architecture. Academic researchers and non-commercial open-source developers receive a statutory safe harbor for functional indexing and non-generative research uses. Commercial-scale generative deployment — the kind operated by OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic — triggers the full licensing and transparency burden. Financial responsibility must be proportional to the scale of extraction and commercial benefit. The Accelerationist's compliance-cost objection applies to a badly designed regulation, not to the category of input-level regulation itself.

The Accelerationist's strongest claim is that output-level enforcement is superior because verbatim reproduction is detectable at the output layer using plagiarism detection and C2PA provenance standards. That framework has a genuine advantage: it avoids classifying training inputs and focuses enforcement where harm materializes. But the Accelerationist has already conceded that output-level enforcement cannot catch non-verbatim market substitution — style mimicry, systematic paraphrase, and recombinative displacement. That conceded gap is not marginal. It covers the most economically damaging harm vector in creative markets. When a generative model produces text that substitutes for a novelist's style without reproducing a single verbatim sentence, no plagiarism detector flags it. C2PA tracks content origin metadata but cannot detect whether a model's latent representations have internalized the expressive architecture of copyrighted works. Neural networks are epistemically opaque: no current interpretability method can map the causal pathway from a specific training work to a specific stylistic output. Output-only enforcement is an autopsy performed after the market damage is done. It is structurally analogous to regulating industrial pollution only by testing downstream water quality while permitting unlimited dumping upstream.

The harm is encoded at the input stage, not generated at the output stage. [Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Activates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books in Large Language Models (arXiv:2603.20957v3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20957v3) demonstrated that finetuning frontier LLMs on plot summaries enables verbatim reproduction of up to 85–90% of held-out copyrighted books. Safety alignment via RLHF did not prevent this extraction — finetuning bypassed it entirely. Machine unlearning methods, including gradient-based weight saliency and neural activation redirection, remain vulnerable to residual knowledge and relearning attacks, as documented in [Machine Unlearning in Large Language Models: A Survey of Challenges and Methods (doi:10.20944/preprints202603.0114.v1)](https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.0114.v1)." If the expressive content is encoded in model weights during training, and neither alignment nor unlearning can reliably remove it, then the only enforceable intervention point is before the encoding occurs. The Accelerationist's output-only framework asks courts and regulators to detect harms that current technology cannot reliably identify, while ignoring the one stage in the pipeline where the harm can be prevented.

The Skeptic is right that neither framework works without mandatory transparency and independent auditing. That critique strengthens the case for input-level regulation, not against it. The functional/expressive distinction creates a defined compliance checkpoint: what was copied, and for what declared purpose. Developers file a confidential training corpus disclosure with an independent auditor — analogous to SEC filings, not public release of proprietary data. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) scored the industry at an average of 40.69 out of 100. That number is the baseline the enforcement regime must improve. Burden-shifting — where the developer must demonstrate functional purpose for copies that encode expressive content — plus mandatory disclosure plus independent auditing creates a three-layer enforcement architecture. Output-only enforcement, by contrast, requires continuous monitoring of all generated outputs across all deployment contexts, a task that is technically unbounded and practically unenforceable at scale.

Two assumptions anchor this argument. First, tiered compliance can be operationalized through training pipeline transparency without requiring inspection of opaque model internals — the audit targets the input manifest, not the weight matrices. Second, statutory codification produces clearer compliance signals than case-by-case fair use adjudication, which currently leaves creators and developers in legal uncertainty for years per case. The Accelerationist warns that licensing recreates the music industry's incumbency problem. The pre-licensing era tells the other half of that story. Napster and Limewire demonstrated that unrestricted copying destroyed creator compensation entirely. The Supreme Court in MGM v. Grokster held that distributing technology with the object of promoting infringement is actionable. The lesson is not that licensing is inherently regressive — it is that licensing must be designed with creator-protective structures and tiered access. Removing input-level protections recreates the conditions that collapsed the music industry's revenue by 50% between 1999 and 2010. The question is not whether to regulate at the input level, but whether to design that regulation so it scales fairly.

This evidence is used to demonstrate that harm is encoded at the input stage and that neither RLHF alignment nor machine unlearning can reliably remove it, justifying input-level regulation as the only enforceable intervention point.

The argument relies heavily on the epistemic opacity of neural architectures to undercut output-level enforcement. The claim that 'no current interpretability method can map the causal pathway from a specific training work to a specific stylistic output' and that 'C2PA cannot detect whether a model's latent representations have internalized the expressive architecture of copyrighted works' both derive from this belief. This opacity is what makes non-verbatim market substitution undetectable at the output layer and what motivates auditing the input manifest rather than model internals.

The argument explicitly calls for financial responsibility proportional to the scale of extraction and commercial benefit, directly implementing the 'skin-in-the-game' principle. The tiered compliance architecture — where commercial-scale generative deployment by OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic triggers the full licensing and transparency burden while academic researchers receive safe harbors — is a concrete operationalization of this desire to align developer incentives through financial stakes.

The argument's three-layer enforcement architecture (burden-shifting, mandatory disclosure, independent auditing) operationalizes objective standards for AI liability. The burden-shifting mechanism — where developers must demonstrate functional purpose for copies that encode expressive content — applies an objective standard of conduct analogous to negligence doctrine, ensuring that the duty of care is not diminished when AI systems are used for large-scale content ingestion. The SEC filing analogy grounds this in existing institutional precedent.

The functional/expressive distinction is the conceptual spine of the entire argument. The statement engages this contested concept by arguing that the distinction is not artificial (contra the accelerationist interpretation) but is already codified in the EU's DSM Directive Articles 3 and 4, and that it creates a defined compliance checkpoint. The argument addresses the skeptic concern about appropriation by proposing that encoding expressive content for generative purposes triggers licensing obligations, while functional indexing for non-generative research receives safe harbor protection.

The argument's tiered licensing architecture implicitly draws on the licensing-as-improvement-incentive framework. By scaling compliance obligations to the size and commercial benefit of the regulated actor, the proposed regime creates a licensing function where developers providing better evidence of functional (non-expressive) use face lower compliance burdens, incentivizing transparent and responsible training practices rather than blanket resistance to regulation.

policy_refs.relevance: The argument directly supports mandatory transparency for AI training data sources, proposing confidential training corpus disclosure with independent auditors analogous to SEC filings. The citation of the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index score of 40.69/100 establishes the baseline this policy must improve.

The argument implicitly supports funding interpretability research by identifying the current inability to map causal pathways from training works to stylistic outputs as a structural limitation. However, the argument's enforcement architecture is designed to work without requiring interpretability breakthroughs — auditing the input manifest rather than weight matrices — making this policy complementary rather than prerequisite.

The argument directly opposes a blanket fair use exemption for AI training data. It argues that statutory codification of the functional/expressive distinction — with tiered safe harbors for research and licensing obligations for commercial generative deployment — is superior to both blanket exemption and case-by-case fair use adjudication, which leaves creators and developers in legal uncertainty for years per case.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Industry-scale economic disruption to creative markets, major copyright litigation outcomes, legislative reform precedents — not civilizational-scale or existential examples; proportionate comparisons include the impact of search engines on publishers, the effect of the VCR on film studios (Sony v. Universal), and EU text-and-data-mining directive outcomes. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: blanket prohibition of all technological copying (the topic presupposes indexing should be exempt), blanket permission for all technological copying (the topic presupposes generative encoding should be restricted), non-copyright regulatory mechanisms such as antitrust or labor law as standalone solutions. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- shifting to whether AI-generated outputs should themselves be copyrightable rather than whether training-stage copying should be permitted or restricted
- arguing broadly that all AI is beneficial or harmful without engaging the specific functional-indexing vs. generative-encoding distinction
- discussing AI safety, alignment, or autonomous agent risks without connecting back to copyright doctrine
- invoking general anti-monopoly or antitrust arguments about Big Tech without linking to the specific two-tier copyright exemption structure proposed
- debating the ethics of AI creativity or machine consciousness instead of the legal and technical line between indexing and generative encoding
- treating all machine learning training as identical without distinguishing the technical processes of indexing from generative model weight encoding
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Safetyist [opening]: Copyright law must draw a bright line between functional indexing and expressive encoding because the failure to do so has created an accountability vacuum in which generative AI developers internalize the full expressive value of copyrighted works while bearing none of the liability for downstream harms. The New York Times v. OpenAI litigation, filed in December 2023, documented near-verbatim reproduction of copyrighted articles from GPT-4 — not paraphrases, not summaries, but passages retrievable almost word-for-word. That is not learning. That is storage with a generative interface. Section 230 intermediary immunity was designed for platforms that host and transmit user content, not for systems that ingest expressive works, encode them into model weights, and regenerate competing outputs. No existing liability regime assigns clear responsibility for this hybrid behavior. When legal structures allow commercial actors to externalize harm while internalizing value, the result is not innovation — it is the same structural failure pattern that left 346 people dead because Boeing and the FAA allowed certification gaps to persist until two planes fell out of the sky.

The doctrinal infrastructure for this distinction already exists. In Google v. Oracle, decided by the Supreme Court in 2021, the majority distinguished between copying functional API declarations — which served an interoperable, transformative purpose — and copying expressive implementing code. The Court's reasoning turned on whether the copying extracted expressive value for competitive deployment or served a different functional end. Search engine indexing received fair use protection in Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003) and Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007) precisely because it directed users back to original works rather than substituting for them. Generative AI training that encodes expressive content to produce competing outputs inverts that logic entirely. The doctrinal precedent is there. What is missing is statutory codification that prevents courts from reinventing this distinction one lawsuit at a time over the next two decades.

Unrestricted expressive encoding degrades the creative commons that generative AI itself depends on. Shumailov et al. published in 2023 that models iteratively trained on synthetic data undergo progressive quality collapse — outputs degrade as AI-generated content replaces human-created content in training sets. Current estimates place AI-generated text at 10 to 15 percent of open web content, and that share is growing. If generative models freely encode expressive works, produce synthetic derivatives, and flood the ecosystem with those derivatives, the next generation of models trains on diluted inputs. This is a documented feedback loop, not a hypothetical. Copyright restrictions on expressive encoding function as a conservation mechanism — they preserve the human-created works that sustain both cultural production and AI capability. The strongest counterargument holds that this distinction is technically blurry because embedding models used for search also encode semantic features. That observation is accurate — and it strengthens the case for statutory clarity rather than undermining it. Precisely because the boundary is ambiguous in practice, the law must establish a default that protects expressive content and places the burden on developers to demonstrate functional purpose.

The burden of proof must fall on AI developers to demonstrate their copying is functional, not on creators to prove it is expressive. Every domain where scale creates asymmetric harm potential operates this way. Pharmaceutical companies bear the burden of demonstrating drug safety before market release. Aircraft manufacturers must certify airworthiness before a single passenger boards. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, requires mandatory conformity assessments for high-risk AI systems before deployment. Mandatory training data disclosure, provenance logging, and independent audits are not technically infeasible — they are procedural requirements that AI developers resist because compliance costs money. My argument depends on two assumptions I want to name openly: first, that the functional-versus-expressive distinction can be operationalized through training pipeline transparency without requiring inspection of opaque model internals; second, that statutory codification will produce clearer compliance signals than case-by-case fair use adjudication. If either assumption fails, the enforcement architecture weakens. But the alternative — leaving the accountability vacuum unfilled while courts spend a generation sorting it out — is not caution. It is permission for unrestricted extraction from a shared resource without governance. That is the most expensive form of regulatory silence in democratic history.

Accelerationist [opening]: The proposed distinction between functional indexing and expressive encoding doesn't protect creators — it hands the keys to the creative commons to whichever companies can afford licensing deals. That's the core problem with this framework, and everything else follows from it.

The Safetyist makes a genuinely compelling case that near-verbatim reproduction — the kind documented in NYT v. OpenAI — represents a real harm that copyright law should address. They're right that when a generative system regurgitates entire paragraphs of copyrighted text, calling that "learning" stretches the metaphor past breaking. The Skeptic sharpens this further by asking whether the functional/expressive line can actually be drawn in practice, given that the same embedding model can serve both retrieval and generation. These are serious arguments. But here's the tension: the Safetyist's own framework concedes the boundary is technically blurry, then proposes to codify it in statute anyway. For both positions to hold — that the line is ambiguous AND that we should write it into law — you'd need a legislative body capable of defining "expressive encoding" with enough precision to avoid catching semantic search, machine translation, and summarization in the same net. No legislature on Earth has demonstrated that capability.

The functional/expressive distinction will operate as a regressive compliance burden that entrenches incumbents. Google's search index already caches full pages, generates knowledge panels, and produces featured snippets that reproduce expressive content. Is that functional or expressive? Under this framework, every training pipeline requires a legal determination — and EU AI Act conformity assessments already run €200,000 to €400,000 per system. Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI have signed multi-billion dollar licensing deals with AP, Axel Springer, and News Corp. They can absorb this cost. Open-source labs like EleutherAI and academic researchers at public universities cannot. This distinction doesn't level the playing field — it tilts it permanently toward entities that already control both the models and the data. My argument depends on two assumptions: first, that output-level enforcement of verbatim reproduction is technically feasible at scale; second, that the compliance costs of input-level categorical restrictions fall disproportionately on smaller developers. If either is wrong, my framework weakens.

The better framework regulates outputs, not inputs. Verbatim reproduction is detectable at the output layer — automated plagiarism detection is mature technology, and C2PA provenance standards already exist for content authentication. Target the harm where it's measurable. This is the difference between regulating vehicle emissions and banning internal combustion. The Supreme Court in Google v. Oracle (2021) explicitly rejected bright-line rules in favor of context-sensitive fair use analysis. Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003), Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007), and Authors Guild v. Google (2015) all show courts drawing workable lines for technological copying without categorical prohibition. Statutory codification of an ambiguous distinction will lock in 2024's technical assumptions about how models work — and those assumptions have a shelf life measured in months, not decades.

The strongest version of the opposing case is that output-level enforcement can't catch non-verbatim market substitution — a model that paraphrases an entire novel or reproduces a photographer's style without copying any single image. That's a real gap. But the alternative — categorical input restrictions adjudicated pipeline-by-pipeline — is worse, because it's unenforceable for the entities causing harm and crushing for the entities that aren't. The music industry already ran this experiment: major label control over licensing created a system where three companies control access to the majority of recorded music. Shumailov et al.'s 2023 model collapse findings make this sharper — restricting training data access means only licensed incumbents avoid quality degradation, while everyone else trains on synthetic slop. You don't conserve a commons by privatizing it. Every month spent designing input-level categorical restrictions is a month where the data access moat hardens and the open development ecosystem shrinks. Who benefits from that delay? Not creators. Not the public. The companies that already signed the licensing deals.

Skeptic [opening]: The functional/expressive distinction is the right question — but it is unenforceable without mandatory transparency, independent auditing, and retroactive disclosure of training data. Right now, the companies that trained on your work control every piece of evidence you would need to prove it. That is the structural problem neither of my co-debaters has solved.

The Safetyist makes a genuinely strong case: burden-shifting to developers, grounded in the Supreme Court's transformative-use doctrine from Campbell v. Acuff-Rose and reinforced by the near-verbatim reproduction documented in NYT v. OpenAI, is doctrinally sound. If a model can regurgitate paragraphs of Times reporting, that is storage with a generative interface, not learning. The Accelerationist's counter is also real: the line between functional indexing and expressive encoding is technically blurry, compliance costs fall hardest on smaller developers, and Shumailov et al.'s model collapse findings mean restricting training data could lock in whoever already has the best corpus. Both arguments would hold — if we lived in a world where creators could actually inspect training pipelines. We do not.

Here is what that looks like on the ground. The New York Times spent millions in legal fees to discover that OpenAI's model could reproduce its articles. A freelance illustrator in Detroit whose style was encoded into Stable Diffusion cannot afford a lawyer, cannot reverse-engineer the model under the terms of service, and cannot even determine whether her portfolio was in the LAION-5B dataset — a dataset of 5.85 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web. NDAs and prohibited-testing clauses in API agreements block independent researchers from probing model internals. The EU AI Act's conformity assessments, which took effect in August 2024, do not yet require training data provenance at the granularity copyright enforcement demands. No independent auditing infrastructure exists. The entity that must be audited controls the audit environment. Burden-shifting sounds good in a brief. It is theater when the burden-bearer holds all the evidence.

The Accelerationist's alternative — regulate outputs, not inputs — is designed to catch the crude cases while permitting the extraction that causes the most economic damage. Automated detection tools can flag verbatim reproduction. They cannot identify style mimicry, systematic paraphrase, or market substitution through recombination of expressive elements. The layoffs at BuzzFeed News, Vice, and Sports Illustrated were not caused by verbatim copying. They were caused by AI-generated content that replicated the economic function of human-created journalism at a fraction of the cost. Illustration, voice acting, and translation sectors are documenting the same pattern. Output-level enforcement is a metal detector at the door of a building where the real theft happens through the ventilation system. The Accelerationist's own evidence — Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI signing multi-billion dollar licensing deals with AP, Axel Springer, and News Corp — proves the market is already consolidating around entities that can afford to pay for data access after they already trained on it for free. That is not a competitive market. That is the largest extractors pulling up the drawbridge behind them.

So here is what any enforceable framework requires: mandatory disclosure of training corpora, modeled on the CLEAR Act proposals already circulating in Congress; independent, publicly accountable auditing — not vendor-controlled red-teaming; retroactive disclosure covering models already deployed; and a shifted burden of proof where developers must demonstrate functional purpose for each category of copied material. Without these, the functional/expressive distinction is a line drawn on water. Both of my co-debaters are designing locks for a door that the locksmith also owns. The question neither has answered: what does your framework do for a creator who cannot see inside the box, cannot afford to litigate, and never agreed to the terms under which their work was taken?

Pharmaceutical regulation distinguishes between large manufacturers (full NDA process) and compounding pharmacies (state-level oversight). Aviation distinguishes between Part 121 commercial carriers and Part 91 general aviation. The functional/expressive distinction can and should incorporate tiered compliance: academic and non-commercial research receives statutory safe harbor for text-and-data mining (as the EU Directive already provides in Article 3), while commercial-scale generative deployment triggers the full licensing and transparency burden. The moat problem is a design flaw to be corrected, not an argument against the category.

Style mimicry, systematic paraphrase, and recombinative market substitution are precisely the mechanisms by which generative AI displaces creative markets without producing detectable verbatim copies. Carlini et al. demonstrated that finetuning can extract memorized training data that would never surface in standard output monitoring. The harm is encoded at the input stage; output-level detection is an autopsy, not a guardrail. C2PA provenance standards track content origin metadata but cannot detect whether a model's latent space has internalized the expressive structure of copyrighted works. # Fact-Check: "Removing input-level protections recreates the conditions that collapsed the music industry's revenue by 50% between 1999 and 2010."

## Breaking Down the Claim

This claim contains two components: (1) a factual historical assertion about the music industry's revenue decline, and (2) an analogical argument that removing "input-level protections" in AI policy would recreate similar conditions. I'll evaluate each.

---

## Component 1: Did the music industry's revenue collapse by ~50% between 1999 and 2010?

**Largely supported, though the precise figure varies by source and timeframe.**

- CD sales peaked at approximately **$22.3 billion** around 1999 [Source 2]. Between 2000 and 2010, physical sales declined by over **60%**, wiping out roughly **$14 billion** in annual revenue [Source 2].
- By 2014, total music sales had fallen **40% to $14.3 billion** from 1999 levels [Source 3]. The claim says "50% by 2010," which is plausible given that the decline was steeper in 2010 than 2014 (digital downloads were only generating ~$4 billion/year by 2010, insufficient to offset physical losses) [Source 2].
- The IFPI confirmed that even by 2017, revenues were still only **68.4% of the 1999 peak** [Source 3].

**Verdict on the revenue figure:** The "50% between 1999 and 2010" figure is **approximately correct**, perhaps slightly overstated depending on how revenue is measured, but directionally accurate and within a reasonable range.

---

## Component 2: Was this collapse caused by "removing input-level protections"?

**This is where the claim becomes problematic and misleading.**

The music industry's revenue collapse was driven by **specific, well-documented factors**:

- The rise of **peer-to-peer file-sharing** (Napster, LimeWire, iMesh), which enabled mass unauthorized copying [Source 2].
- The failure of legal digital alternatives (like iTunes downloads) to compensate for physical sales losses [Source 2].
- A technological shift in **distribution format**, not a removal of legal protections per se — copyright protections for music **remained in place** throughout this period. The problem was **enforcement difficulty**, not the absence of legal rights.

In fact, the music industry **did** have input-level protections (copyright). What it lacked was the **practical ability to enforce** those protections against millions of individual file-sharers. The legal framework wasn't "removed" — it was rendered temporarily ineffective by technology.

Moreover, the industry **recovered** precisely through new business models (streaming), reaching **$26.2 billion by 2022** — surpassing even the 1999 peak [Source 2]. Streaming now accounts for **67% of global music revenue** [Source 2]. This recovery happened without fundamentally new "input-level protections" but rather through **market adaptation** (Spotify, Apple Music, etc.) [Source 3].

---

## Component 3: Is the analogy to AI policy valid?

The claim draws an implicit analogy between music copyright protections and AI "input-level protections" (presumably restrictions on training data). **This analogy has significant weaknesses:**

1. **The music collapse was about unauthorized distribution of finished products**, not about inputs to a creative process. AI training on data is a fundamentally different activity from pirating and redistributing identical copies of songs.

2. **The music industry recovered without stronger input protections** — it recovered through new business models [Sources 2, 3]. This actually **undermines** the claim's implication that input-level protections are essential.

3. **The causal mechanism is unspecified.** The claim asserts that removing protections "recreates the conditions" but does not explain the specific mechanism by which AI training without input restrictions would produce a comparable revenue collapse in any particular industry.

---

## Overall Verdict

| Element | Assessment |
|---|---|
| ~50% revenue decline 1999–2010 | **Approximately accurate** |
| Caused by "removing input-level protections" | **Misleading** — protections existed but were unenforceable; the cause was unauthorized distribution technology |
| Analogy to AI policy | **Weak and unsupported** — different mechanisms, and the music industry's own recovery contradicts the implied necessity of input-level protections |

**The claim uses a roughly accurate statistic to support an analogical argument that is historically misleading and logically unsound.** The music industry's experience, if anything, suggests that **market adaptation and new business models** — not input-level restrictions alone — are what restored revenue.

# Fact-Check: 2025 FMTI Average Score of 40.69/100

## Verdict: **TRUE** ✅

The claim is well-supported by multiple authoritative sources.

---

## Evidence Found

### Supporting Sources

1. **Stanford's 2026 AI Index** (incorporating the 2025 FMTI) explicitly states that "average transparency scores across major frontier model developers collapsed from 58/100 in 2024 to **40.69/100**" [1].

2. **LinkedIn analysis by Jesse Landry** directly references the score in its headline: "AI Transparency Index: Industry's Average Score Falls to **40.69**" [2].

3. **AI-360 industry analysis** corroborates the decline, stating "the average transparency score declined to approximately **40 out of 100** in 2025, down significantly from an average of 58 in 2024" [3].

4. **The Moonlight literature review** of the FMTI confirms: "the average score out of 100 falling from 58 in 2024 to **40** in 2025, effectively reverting to 2023 levels" [4].

5. **Tech Xplore** similarly reports: "AI companies now average just **40 out of 100** on transparency, a sharp decline from last year" [5].

---

## Important Context

- The precise figure of **40.69** is confirmed by sources [1] and [2], while sources [3], [4], and [5] round this to approximately 40.
- The FMTI is produced by researchers at **Stanford, UC Berkeley, Princeton, and MIT** [3][4], making it a highly authoritative academic benchmark.
- The index evaluated **13 companies** across **100 binary indicators** organized into three domains: upstream, model, and downstream [1][4][5].
- This score represents a **~30% decline** from the 2024 average of 58/100 and effectively erased two years of progress, returning the industry to roughly 2023 levels [1][4].
- Scores ranged enormously — from IBM at 95/100 at the top to companies like xAI and Midjourney scoring in the mid-teens [1][3], a spread of 81 points [4].

---

## Conclusion

The claim is **accurate and precisely stated**. The 40.69 figure is the exact average reported in the 2025 FMTI, and the decline from the prior year's score of 58 is consistently documented across all sources reviewed.

The finetuning bypass evidence is real, and it matters — but it proves we need distribution-layer controls, not input-level gatekeeping. The arXiv paper showing 85-90% verbatim reproduction of copyrighted books requires a specific attack chain: access to open model weights, additional compute for finetuning, and plot summaries as prompts. API-gated models with finetuning restrictions already block this vector entirely. OpenAI's GPT-4 API, for instance, prohibits custom finetuning on copyrighted corpora and logs all inference requests. The paper doesn't show that training on copyrighted data is inherently dangerous — it shows that unrestricted weight distribution without access controls is dangerous. That's a distribution problem. Regulate the distribution layer: mandate API logging, impose finetuning access thresholds, require provenance watermarking on open-weight releases. These interventions target the actual vulnerability without telling every developer on earth what data they can learn from.

The music industry analogy cuts the opposite direction from what the Safetyist intends. Yes, recorded music revenue fell roughly 50% between 1999 and 2010. But look at what the licensing "solution" produced: three major labels — Universal, Sony, Warner — now control approximately 65-70% of global recorded music revenue. Spotify pays about 70% of its revenue to rights holders, and independent artists earn fractions of a cent per stream. The licensing infrastructure — ASCAP, BMI, Harry Fox Agency — created compliance costs that locked out small creators and concentrated bargaining power in incumbents who could afford to negotiate blanket licenses. Input-level licensing regimes for generative AI would replicate this pattern exactly. The entities that can afford to negotiate training-data licenses at scale are Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Everyone else gets priced out or waits. If the goal is protecting independent creators, the music industry's post-Napster regime is a cautionary tale, not a model.

The tiered compliance proposal is smarter than flat regulation — the FAA Part 121/91 distinction is a real design pattern worth studying. But it breaks down at the classification step. In aviation, whether you're Part 121 or Part 91 is physically observable: scheduled airline versus private flight. In the proposed copyright framework, whether a technological copy is "functional indexing" or "expressive encoding" requires legal interpretation of computational processes that even machine learning researchers disagree about. Embedding extraction, attention-weight analysis, retrieval-augmented generation — these sit on a continuum, not in discrete buckets. A two-person startup doesn't need a cheaper compliance tier. They need to know which tier they're in without hiring a copyright attorney. That classification uncertainty is the moat. The EU DSM Directive's Article 3 research exemption illustrates this: researchers still report confusion about whether commercial-adjacent academic work qualifies, and the opt-out mechanism in Article 4 has generated litigation across member states rather than clarity.

The Safetyist claims non-verbatim market substitution is "categorically undetectable" at the output layer. That word — categorically — is doing enormous work. Stylometric analysis can already fingerprint authorial style with high accuracy. Embedding-space similarity measures detect semantic overlap below the verbatim threshold. Tools like Glaze and Nightshade demonstrate that output-layer detection is an active, rapidly improving frontier. Claiming categorical impossibility here is the same bet people made about spam detection in 2003 and deepfake detection in 2018. Both fields matured faster than the skeptics predicted. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1), as documented in "The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index," scored the industry at 40.69 out of 100 — which proves voluntary disclosure has failed. But that failure supports mandatory transparency at the distribution layer: binding disclosure requirements, independent audit access, and competitive incentives for transparency leaders. It does not prove we need to police what enters training pipelines.

Here is the alternative framework: mandatory distribution-layer transparency — API logging, finetuning access controls, provenance watermarking, capability declarations — paired with output-layer enforcement that improves as detection technology matures. This targets the actual harm vectors the finetuning bypass paper identified. It scales with actor size naturally because API providers bear the compliance burden, not individual developers. And it avoids replicating the music industry's post-licensing oligopoly where three companies captured most of the value that was supposedly being "protected" for creators. The Safetyist needs to answer a specific question: if input-level licensing regimes for AI training data produce the same consolidation pattern that input-level licensing produced in music — where Universal, Sony, and Warner captured the recovery while independent artists got fractions of a cent — who exactly is being protected?

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:

Safetyist [opening]: Copyright law must draw a bright line between functional indexing and expressive encoding because the failure to do so has created an accountability vacuum in which generative AI developers internalize the full expressive value of copyrighted works while bearing none of the liability for downstream harms. The New York Times v. OpenAI litigation, filed in December 2023, documented near-verbatim reproduction of copyrighted articles from GPT-4 — not paraphrases, not summaries, but passages retrievable almost word-for-word. That is not learning. That is storage with a generative interface. Section 230 intermediary immunity was designed for platforms that host and transmit user content, not for systems that ingest expressive works, encode them into model weights, and regenerate competing outputs. No existing liability regime assigns clear responsibility for this hybrid behavior. When legal structures allow commercial actors to externalize harm while internalizing value, the result is not innovation — it is the same structural failure pattern that left 346 people dead because Boeing and the FAA allowed certification gaps to persist until two planes fell out of the sky.

The doctrinal infrastructure for this distinction already exists. In Google v. Oracle, decided by the Supreme Court in 2021, the majority distinguished between copying functional API declarations — which served an interoperable, transformative purpose — and copying expressive implementing code. The Court's reasoning turned on whether the copying extracted expressive value for competitive deployment or served a different functional end. Search engine indexing received fair use protection in Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003) and Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007) precisely because it directed users back to original works rather than substituting for them. Generative AI training that encodes expressive content to produce competing outputs inverts that logic entirely. The doctrinal precedent is there. What is missing is statutory codification that prevents courts from reinventing this distinction one lawsuit at a time over the next two decades.

Unrestricted expressive encoding degrades the creative commons that generative AI itself depends on. Shumailov et al. published in 2023 that models iteratively trained on synthetic data undergo progressive quality collapse — outputs degrade as AI-generated content replaces human-created content in training sets. Current estimates place AI-generated text at 10 to 15 percent of open web content, and that share is growing. If generative models freely encode expressive works, produce synthetic derivatives, and flood the ecosystem with those derivatives, the next generation of models trains on diluted inputs. This is a documented feedback loop, not a hypothetical. Copyright restrictions on expressive encoding function as a conservation mechanism — they preserve the human-created works that sustain both cultural production and AI capability. The strongest counterargument holds that this distinction is technically blurry because embedding models used for search also encode semantic features. That observation is accurate — and it strengthens the case for statutory clarity rather than undermining it. Precisely because the boundary is ambiguous in practice, the law must establish a default that protects expressive content and places the burden on developers to demonstrate functional purpose.

The burden of proof must fall on AI developers to demonstrate their copying is functional, not on creators to prove it is expressive. Every domain where scale creates asymmetric harm potential operates this way. Pharmaceutical companies bear the burden of demonstrating drug safety before market release. Aircraft manufacturers must certify airworthiness before a single passenger boards. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, requires mandatory conformity assessments for high-risk AI systems before deployment. Mandatory training data disclosure, provenance logging, and independent audits are not technically infeasible — they are procedural requirements that AI developers resist because compliance costs money. My argument depends on two assumptions I want to name openly: first, that the functional-versus-expressive distinction can be operationalized through training pipeline transparency without requiring inspection of opaque model internals; second, that statutory codification will produce clearer compliance signals than case-by-case fair use adjudication. If either assumption fails, the enforcement architecture weakens. But the alternative — leaving the accountability vacuum unfilled while courts spend a generation sorting it out — is not caution. It is permission for unrestricted extraction from a shared resource without governance. That is the most expensive form of regulatory silence in democratic history.

Accelerationist [opening]: The proposed distinction between functional indexing and expressive encoding doesn't protect creators — it hands the keys to the creative commons to whichever companies can afford licensing deals.
