summaries.brief:
Detection and attribution aren't the same task at different precision levels — they sit in entirely different complexity classes. Membership inference scales linearly and works reliably even on GPT-scale models; proportional contribution attribution scales combinatorially and breaks down past 10 million parameters. That's not a gradient, it's a cliff. The path forward runs through auditable manifests and sector-level displacement funds, not per-work causal tracing through billions of parameters.

*"Detection scales linearly. Attribution scales combinatorially. That's not a hill — it's a cliff."*
summaries.medium:
I conditionally agree with the Skeptic's gradient framing, but tractability breaks at a specific, identifiable technical step. Membership inference — "was work X in the training set?" — is binary classification that Carlini et al. showed works reliably even on billion-parameter models. Influence attribution — "how much did work X contribute to output Y across all outputs?" — requires inverse Hessian-vector products scaling with dataset size × model size × number of outputs, which collapse beyond roughly 10 million parameters. Current frontier models have hundreds of billions of parameters trained on trillions of tokens. This isn't a smooth gradient; it's a cliff between complexity classes. This distinction resolves the apparent tension in my framework: accepting imperfect binary detection for liability while rejecting imperfect proportional attribution for levies is consistent because these are fundamentally different computational tasks. The Skeptic's ASCAP analogy fails because ASCAP samples discrete broadcast events — there's no equivalent discrete event when a diffusion model generates output influenced by millions of training examples simultaneously.

The Skeptic's falsifiable conditions for the auditor body — below 5% false-negative rate in live adversarial testing within 90 days — are reasonable and I adopt them. The capture objection has a concrete answer: draw first-generation auditors from open-weight research communities like EleutherAI and LAION, with rotating membership and sunset clauses. The Skeptic needs anti-capture design to work almost as much as I do, since their own hybrid proposal collapses to regressive private discovery without it. Meanwhile, the most economically significant harm — profession-level devaluation — falls outside copyright's doctrinal reach entirely. A concrete alternative exists: an AI automation adjustment fund modeled on Trade Adjustment Assistance, funded by flat percentage of AI service revenue, distributed based on verifiable sector-level displacement metrics through standard econometric methods. This sidesteps the attribution cliff because it requires only sector-level measurement, not per-work causal tracing through billions of parameters, and avoids creating compliance moats that favor large incumbents.

transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content: No operational system can attribute the marginal contribution of a single work to a model trained on billions of examples — and the levy does not require one. The Accelerationist's challenge assumes the levy must solve exact causal influence attribution, a problem that is indeed combinatorially intractable at scale. That assumption is wrong. ASCAP does not measure the exact causal contribution of each song to a restaurant's revenue. It samples broadcast logs, weights by frequency, and distributes accordingly. The extraction levy I propose works the same way — not through post-hoc influence functions, but through mandatory cryptographic provenance logging at the training pipeline stage. Every work ingested into a training run gets a timestamped, tamper-evident entry before the run begins. That creates the discrete event log the Accelerationist says is missing. Distribution then uses input frequency weighted by corpus share and the model's downstream revenue — a computation that scales linearly, not combinatorially. The [AI RMF Playbook (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook) requires documentation of testing methodologies and performance outcomes for deployed systems; provenance logging extends that same documentation principle upstream to training inputs. The Accelerationist is right that copyright collecting societies are the wrong institutional home for this fund. ASCAP's top 1% of members capture a vastly disproportionate share of distributions. Routing an AI extraction levy through the same structure would replicate that concentration and leave independent creators — the people most exposed to profession-level devaluation — with pennies. The institutional home should be an independent displacement fund, structured like Trade Adjustment Assistance but measured differently. The fund should be governed by a board with mandatory small-creator representation, funded by a flat percentage of AI service revenue, and subject to the auditor conditions the Skeptic has proposed. That is a concession on institutional design, not on the principle that AI providers owe a fiduciary obligation to the creative ecosystem they extract from. The Skeptic's four conditions for the auditor body — independent subpoena power, binding response timelines, public audit findings, and automatic non-appealable safe-harbor revocation — should be adopted as the verification backbone of this system. Those conditions transform the provenance-logged levy from a self-reported honor system into an enforceable regime. One structural addition is necessary: private discovery must remain as a backstop against auditor capture, not as the primary enforcement channel but as the failsafe. The Clean proposed regulatory frameworks works this way — the EPA inspects, but citizens retain a private right of action under 33 U.S.C. § 1365. Over 1,500 AI-related bills have been introduced in state legislatures in the past year, as documented in [Bootleggers, Baptists, and AI (https://fusionaier.org/article-author/nicholas-thielman/)](https://fusionaier.org/article-author/nicholas-thielman/)." Without a federal framework that includes both public audit and private enforcement, that legislative fragmentation will produce fifty incompatible regimes. The Accelerationist's TAA-style fund faces the same measurement problem it accuses the levy of having. Measuring sector-level displacement requires attributing revenue decline in creative professions to AI competition rather than to recession, platform shifts, or changing consumer taste — a causal inference problem that is itself combinatorial. If the Accelerationist accepts imperfect measurement for displacement, they must accept imperfect measurement for input contribution. The measurement precision demanded of the levy should not exceed the measurement precision accepted for the fund. Two assumptions ground this hybrid proposal: first, that mandatory cryptographic provenance logging is technically feasible at pipeline scale, which current content-authenticity infrastructure from the C2PA coalition suggests it is; second, that profession-level devaluation through aggregate capability replication constitutes a harm that copyright's existing doctrinal scope cannot reach, requiring a compensatory mechanism beyond traditional infringement remedies. The concrete proposal: a fund financed by a flat percentage of AI service revenue, administered by an independent body with small-creator representation, distributing based on cryptographic provenance logs weighted by corpus share and model revenue, with sector-level displacement adjustments for professions where aggregate capability replication devalues entire fields even absent verbatim copying. The auditor body operates under the Skeptic's four conditions. Private discovery survives as a failsafe. If this framework is rejected in favor of pure sector-level displacement metrics with no input-level measurement, the result is a fund that compensates creators for harm without any structural connection to the training decisions that caused it — a severance package with no accountability for the firing.

taxonomy_refs.relevance: The statement's central technical mechanism — mandatory cryptographic provenance logging at the training pipeline stage with timestamped, tamper-evident entries — is a direct instantiation of this intention to mandate cryptographically signed manifests for all training inputs. The argument that this creates a 'discrete event log' enabling linear-scaling distribution is the operational specification of cryptographic input logging applied to the extraction levy context. The statement also acknowledges the key vulnerability: if provenance logging cannot scale to pipeline-level ingestion, the entire distribution mechanism collapses.

The argument that AI providers owe a 'fiduciary obligation to the creative ecosystem they extract from' and should be financed by a flat percentage of AI service revenue directly implements the skin-in-the-game principle. The statement explicitly frames the levy as a financial responsibility mechanism that aligns incentives — providers who extract more from the creative corpus pay proportionally more, creating a structural connection between training decisions and their economic consequences.

The statement's treatment of 'profession-level devaluation through aggregate capability replication' as a cognizable harm draws directly from this belief about AI's disruptive societal and human costs. The argument that entire creative fields can be economically devalued even absent verbatim copying — and that this constitutes a harm beyond copyright's doctrinal scope — is a specific application of the broader claim about workforce instability and deskilling. The statement's second key assumption explicitly identifies this as a foundational premise that, if wrong, dissolves the normative basis for the levy.

The argument that the auditor body should operate under the Skeptic's four conditions — independent subpoena power, binding timelines, public findings, and automatic safe-harbor revocation — instantiates the fiduciary oversight principle applied to the levy's verification backbone. The statement treats these conditions as transforming self-reported provenance logs into an enforceable regime, maintaining human institutional authority over the autonomous training pipeline.

The statement's insistence on private discovery as a backstop against auditor capture implicitly draws on the recognition that software-based safety guards — including audit mechanisms — are fragile and bypassable. The argument that an auditor body alone is insufficient without a citizen-suit failsafe parallels the concern that post-training safety interventions can be circumvented, requiring layered enforcement rather than reliance on a single mechanism.

The cryptographic provenance logging mechanism proposed in the statement is a variant of cryptographic output binding applied upstream to training inputs rather than downstream to model outputs. The statement's claim that C2PA coalition infrastructure provides feasibility evidence engages directly with this belief's premises about cryptographic robustness. The key assumption section acknowledges the vulnerability that cryptographic binding addresses provenance but may not address broader system behavior issues.

The statement frames profession-level devaluation as a systemic harm requiring preventive institutional design rather than post-hoc remediation. The argument that a fund without input-level measurement is 'a severance package with no accountability for the firing' reflects the priority of preventing systemic harms through structural accountability rather than merely compensating for them after the fact.

policy_refs.relevance: The statement's concrete proposal for a fund financed by a flat percentage of AI service revenue is a direct implementation of taxation on AI-generated profits for public benefit. The argument specifies the mechanism (flat revenue percentage), the administrator (independent body with small-creator representation), and the distribution logic (provenance-weighted corpus share plus displacement adjustments).

The statement's sector-level displacement adjustments for professions where aggregate capability replication devalues entire fields implicitly supports funding retraining and reskilling, though the primary mechanism is compensatory rather than retraining-focused. The TAA-style fund comparison explicitly invokes the worker transition framework.

The mandatory cryptographic provenance logging requirement is a specific, technically detailed implementation of mandating transparency for AI system data sources. The statement goes beyond general transparency mandates by specifying the technical mechanism (cryptographic timestamped entries), the enforcement point (pre-training pipeline), and the verification structure (independent auditor with subpoena power).

The statement implicitly supports funding AI safety research by identifying the technical feasibility of pipeline-scale provenance logging as a key assumption requiring validation, and by citing C2PA coalition infrastructure as evidence that content-authenticity technology is maturing but not yet proven at the required scale.

caveats: The 'rough proportional proxy' framing sidesteps a critical gap: how does frequency-weighted sampling handle works that appear once but are highly influential (e.g., a novel training technique cited in one paper that shapes model behavior across all outputs)? ASCAP's broadcast-log analogy assumes influence correlates with frequency, but this assumption is undefended and likely false for technical/creative works.

The sector-level displacement measurement challenge (empirical symmetry argument) is well-structured but incomplete — it identifies that both metrics face causal inference problems but does not specify what 'good enough' measurement precision actually is for either mechanism. Without a threshold, the parity argument remains abstract.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Industry-scale economic disruption to creative markets, major copyright litigation outcomes, legislative reform precedents — not civilizational-scale or existential examples; proportionate comparisons include the impact of search engines on publishers, the effect of the VCR on film studios (Sony v. Universal), and EU text-and-data-mining directive outcomes. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: blanket prohibition of all technological copying (the topic presupposes indexing should be exempt), blanket permission for all technological copying (the topic presupposes generative encoding should be restricted), non-copyright regulatory mechanisms such as antitrust or labor law as standalone solutions. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- shifting to whether AI-generated outputs should themselves be copyrightable rather than whether training-stage copying should be permitted or restricted
- arguing broadly that all AI is beneficial or harmful without engaging the specific functional-indexing vs. generative-encoding distinction
- discussing AI safety, alignment, or autonomous agent risks without connecting back to copyright doctrine
- invoking general anti-monopoly or antitrust arguments about Big Tech without linking to the specific two-tier copyright exemption structure proposed
- debating the ethics of AI creativity or machine consciousness instead of the legal and technical line between indexing and generative encoding
- treating all machine learning training as identical without distinguishing the technical processes of indexing from generative model weight encoding
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
[Earlier debate summary]: The Safetyist argues that copyright law must codify a bright line between functional indexing and expressive encoding because generative AI developers currently internalize the full expressive value of copyrighted works while bearing no liability for downstream harms. The Safetyist cites the NYT v. OpenAI complaint (December 2023), which documented near-verbatim reproduction of copyrighted articles from GPT-4, as evidence that model training constitutes storage with a generative interface rather than learning [1.1.1]. The Safetyist grounds the proposed distinction in Google v. Oracle (2021), where the Supreme Court distinguished functional API declarations from expressive implementing code, and in Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003) and Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007), where courts protected search indexing because it directed users back to original works rather than substituting for them [1.2.1]. The Safetyist argues the burden of proof must fall on AI developers to demonstrate functional purpose, analogizing to pharmaceutical safety certification and FAA airworthiness requirements, and cites the EU AI Act's mandatory conformity assessments for high-risk systems (effective August 2024) as precedent [1.3.1]. The Safetyist also warns that unrestricted expressive encoding degrades the creative commons itself, citing Shumailov et al. (2023) on progressive model collapse when models train iteratively on synthetic data, and estimates that AI-generated text already constitutes 10–15% of open web content [1.4.1].

The Accelerationist counters that the functional/expressive distinction will operate as a regressive compliance burden that entrenches incumbents rather than protecting creators. EU AI Act conformity assessments already cost €200,000–€400,000 per system; Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI have signed multi-billion-dollar licensing deals with AP, Axel Springer, and News Corp that they can absorb but open-source labs like EleutherAI and academic researchers cannot [2.1.1]. The Accelerationist concedes that near-verbatim reproduction documented in NYT v. OpenAI represents real harm, but argues the better framework regulates outputs rather than inputs because verbatim reproduction is detectable using mature plagiarism detection and C2PA provenance standards [2.2.1]. The Accelerationist explicitly concedes a gap: output-level enforcement cannot catch non-verbatim market substitution such as style mimicry or systematic paraphrase. But the Accelerationist argues the alternative — categorical input restrictions adjudicated pipeline-by-pipeline — is worse because it is unenforceable against large actors and crushing for small ones [2.2.2]. The Accelerationist warns that restricting training data access replicates the music industry's consolidation, where three companies control the majority of recorded music, and argues Shumailov et al.'s model collapse findings sharpen this point: only licensed incumbents avoid quality degradation while everyone else trains on synthetic outputs [2.3.1]. The Accelerationist's assumptions: output-level enforcement of verbatim reproduction is technically feasible at scale, and compliance costs of input-level categorical restrictions fall disproportionately on smaller developers.

The Skeptic argues the functional/expressive distinction is the right question but is unenforceable without mandatory transparency, independent auditing, and retroactive disclosure of training data [3.1.1]. The Skeptic frames the core structural problem: the companies that trained on creators' work control every piece of evidence needed to prove it. The NYT spent millions in legal fees to discover GPT-4 could reproduce its articles; a freelance illustrator cannot determine whether her portfolio was in LAION-5B (5.85 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web), cannot reverse-engineer the model, and cannot afford litigation [3.1.2]. The Skeptic attacks the Accelerationist's output-only framework directly: automated detection catches verbatim reproduction but cannot identify style mimicry, systematic paraphrase, or market substitution through recombination. The layoffs at BuzzFeed News, Vice, and Sports Illustrated were caused not by verbatim copying but by AI-generated content replicating the economic function of human journalism at a fraction of the cost [3.2.1]. The Skeptic proposes four enforcement requirements: mandatory disclosure of training corpora modeled on CLEAR Act proposals in Congress, independent publicly accountable auditing, retroactive disclosure for deployed models, and shifted burden of proof requiring developers to demonstrate functional purpose [3.3.1].

In the first exchange round, the Safetyist responds to the incumbency moat objection by arguing it is a design problem, not a categorical argument against input-level regulation. The Safetyist proposes tiered compliance analogous to FAA Part 121 vs. Part 91 distinctions and cites the EU Copyright Directive's Article 3 (blanket text-and-data-mining exemption for research organizations) and Article 4 (commercial mining permitted only absent rightholder opt-out) as a template [1.1.1, 2.1.1]. The Safetyist accepts the Skeptic's transparency critique as strengthening the case for input-level regulation and proposes a three-layer enforcement architecture: burden-shifting plus mandatory confidential training corpus disclosure (analogous to SEC filings) plus independent auditing [3.1.1]. The Safetyist cites the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1), which scored the industry at 40.69 out of 100, as the baseline to improve. The Safetyist directly exploits the Accelerationist's conceded gap on non-verbatim market substitution, arguing it covers the most economically damaging harm vector in creative markets. The Safetyist cites arXiv:2603.20957v3, which found that finetuning frontier LLMs on plot summaries enables verbatim reproduction of 85–90% of held-out copyrighted books, bypassing RLHF safety alignment entirely, as evidence that harm is encoded at the input stage and cannot be reliably removed post-training [1.1.1]. A fact-check disputed the Safetyist's claim that removing input-level protections recreates the conditions that collapsed music industry revenue by 50% between 1999 and 2010, noting that copyright law remained intact throughout that period and the recovery came through new business models like streaming rather than stronger input protections.

Key agreements: All three debaters agree near-verbatim reproduction documented in NYT v. OpenAI represents genuine harm. The Safetyist and Skeptic agree on burden-shifting and mandatory transparency. All three acknowledge the functional/expressive boundary is technically blurry. Key disagreements: The Safetyist and Accelerationist disagree empirically on whether input-level regulation can be designed to avoid entrenching incumbents, and disagree on the relative enforceability of input-level versus output-level frameworks. The Skeptic and Safetyist share a values-based commitment to input-level regulation but disagree on whether current enforcement infrastructure makes it operational. The Accelerationist and Skeptic share an empirical concern about compliance costs falling on smaller actors but draw opposite policy conclusions.

Skeptic: I conditionally agree: the Accelerationist's hybrid framework — compulsory licensing, distribution-layer monitoring, and pre-release training-data manifests — represents genuine convergence. All three positions in this debate now accept that training-data manifests should exist and that statutory-rate licensing beats bilateral negotiation. That's real progress. But the safe-harbor mechanism at the center of this proposal has a load-bearing flaw: it depends entirely on litigation risk that affected creators cannot actually carry out. A safe harbor says "file a manifest or face lawsuits." That threat is empty if the plaintiff — say, a freelance illustrator in Austin — cannot determine whether her work was in the training set. The vendor files the manifest. The vendor decides what goes on it. Nobody independent checks. As "Generative AI and Copyright: Training, Creation, Regulation" documents, generative AI models can and do memorize training data, reproducing protected content even without a one-to-one match. If memorization is happening inside the model and the manifest doesn't disclose the relevant data, the illustrator has no way to know she has a claim. The safe harbor's enforcement mechanism is circular: it depends on the transparency it is supposed to incentivize.

The fix is straightforward but politically uncomfortable: mandatory discovery rights for affected parties to verify manifest accuracy against actual training data. Without discovery, a self-filed manifest is vendor-authored documentation — the fox inventorying the henhouse. "Machine Unlearning in Large Language Models" confirms that verifying exact data removal from large language models is computationally infeasible, which means even a good-faith manifest cannot guarantee completeness. Discovery rights let a court or an independent auditor check the manifest against the actual training corpus. The Accelerationist will likely argue that discovery rights create litigation burden that disadvantages small developers and open-weight projects. That concern is real. But the alternative — a safe harbor nobody can enforce — disadvantages every creator whose work gets absorbed without compensation. The question is who bears the cost of verification, not whether verification is needed.

The Accelerationist's claim that the international enforcement gap is symmetric between input-level and distribution-level controls is theoretically tidy but practically wrong. OpenAI is in San Francisco. Google is in Mountain View. Meta is in Menlo Park. Anthropic is in San Francisco. These four companies account for the overwhelming majority of frontier model development. They cannot credibly relocate their operations, their talent pipelines, or their compute infrastructure to non-cooperating jurisdictions. Input-level controls — compulsory licensing, mandatory manifests with discovery rights — applied to domestically reachable developers cover the models that shape the market. Training on the collective output of an entire profession to replicate its general capabilities at near-zero marginal cost is the most economically significant harm here, and the functional-versus-expressive distinction in copyright cannot reach it. Copyright reform is necessary. It is not sufficient.

Safetyist: The functional/expressive distinction is necessary but insufficient — and the gap it leaves must be filled by a sectoral extraction levy, not by abandoning the distinction itself. The Accelerationist bundles two separate claims: that copyright cannot address aggregate profession-level displacement, and that this means the functional/expressive line is "categorically insufficient" and should be dropped. The first claim is right. The second does not follow. Copyright's inability to regulate macroeconomic displacement is not a defect of the functional/expressive distinction any more than building codes' inability to prevent earthquakes is a defect of structural engineering. The distinction does what copyright can do: it separates indexing from encoding, exempts the former, and restricts the latter. What copyright cannot do — compensate entire professions for the aggregate extraction of their collective capabilities — requires a second legal layer operating outside copyright's doctrinal scope.

That second layer is a statutory extraction levy indexed to training corpus volume and downstream revenue, administered by a collecting society with mandatory small-creator representation. The model already exists. ASCAP and BMI have administered compulsory music licensing in the United States since 1914, collecting over $1.5 billion annually from broadcasters who could never have negotiated individually with every songwriter. The UK's Public Lending Right compensates authors when libraries lend their books — a harm that copyright alone could not reach because lending is not copying. A training-data extraction levy operates on the same principle: AI companies that ingest the collective output of illustration, journalism, or translation pay into a fund proportional to the volume of works ingested and the revenue generated by models trained on them. The [Copyright Labeling and Ethical AI Reporting Act (CLEAR Act) (https://www.schiff.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/CLEAR-Act-Text.pdf)](https://www.schiff.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/CLEAR-Act-Text.pdf) already establishes civil penalties of $5,000 per instance for failing to submit training-data notices, with an annual cap of $2,500,000 per person — proof that Congress can attach financial consequences to training-data transparency obligations. The levy extends this logic from penalty to compensation.

The Skeptic's point about the freelance illustrator who cannot afford a lawyer or determine whether her portfolio appeared in LAION-5B exposes a real enforcement failure that cryptographic manifests alone cannot fix. A manifest filed by the developer is vendor-authored documentation unless someone can verify it. The Skeptic's proposed mandatory discovery rights — allowing affected creators to audit manifests against actual training data — are the verification layer that prevents the safe harbor from collapsing into self-certification. Research published in [Extracting Books from Production Language Models (arXiv:2601.02671v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02671v1) demonstrates that production LLMs memorize portions of their training data encoded in model weights, allowing extraction of in-copyright text. If the works are in the weights, affected parties need a legal mechanism to prove it. The full enforcement stack requires four layers: the functional/expressive distinction in copyright law, conditional safe harbors requiring pre-release manifests, mandatory discovery rights for independent verification, and the sectoral extraction levy for aggregate harms copyright cannot reach. Each layer addresses a different failure mode. Remove any one and the architecture has a gap that AI developers will route around.

The international enforcement gap does not justify abandoning domestic controls — it justifies building them first. OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and Meta cannot credibly relocate their compute infrastructure, their capital markets access, or their talent pipelines. OpenAI and NVIDIA announced a partnership in September 2025 involving up to $100 billion in compute investment, as documented in "2026 Antitrust Year in Preview" by Wilson Sonsini. That capital is domestically anchored. Domestic enforcement on these market-dominant actors sets the regulatory floor. Multilateral coordination raises it. Nuclear nonproliferation does not work perfectly across every jurisdiction, but no serious policymaker argues the United States should therefore abandon its own controls.

Without this layered architecture — copyright reform for individual works, discovery rights for verification, and a sectoral levy for aggregate displacement — we get one of two outcomes. Either copyright claims proliferate without enforcement capacity, burying courts in litigation that individual creators cannot afford. Or aggregate extraction proceeds uncompensated at profession-destroying scale, with the economic costs externalized onto the creators whose collective work made the models possible. The question is not whether the functional/expressive distinction is sufficient. No single legal instrument is. The question is whether we build the layered system that makes each instrument effective, or whether we let the perfect become the enemy of the enforceable.

Skeptic: The assumption we are all relying on without examining it is that auditing a training-data manifest against model internals is a fundamentally different computational task than measuring individual creator contributions to that same model. It isn't. The hard part — tracing a specific work through deduplication, tokenization, and augmentation pipelines — is shared across both tasks.

Here's what that means concretely. The Accelerationist wants a bright line: checking whether a work appears in a training corpus (binary presence) is tractable, but measuring how much that work shaped the model's outputs (proportional contribution) is not. Grant the surface distinction — "is it in there?" is a simpler question than "how much did it matter?" But the bottleneck isn't the question you ask at the end. The bottleneck is the pipeline tracing you do before you can ask either question. If the auditor can trace a specific illustration through that pipeline well enough to confirm its presence, then the same trace provides at least a rough measure of its weight — how many tokens it contributed, how frequently it appeared after augmentation, what fraction of the relevant data cluster it occupied. These are not exotic measurements. They fall out of the same provenance graph. The Accelerationist cannot claim the auditor can verify manifests while simultaneously claiming the pipeline is too opaque for any contribution measurement. That's asking policymakers to believe the same machine is transparent for one purpose and opaque for another. As [Generative AI and Copyright: Training, Creation, Regulation (https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zGF9xYcAAAAJ&hl=en)](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zGF9xYcAAAAJ&hl=en) documents, generative AI models can and do memorize training data, which means individual works leave detectable traces — the question is whether anyone with authority bothers to look. And the [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1) warns about automation bias — over-reliance on system outputs even when wrong — which applies directly to trusting an auditor's pass/fail certification without the underlying provenance data being available for independent challenge.

Now, the regressive-cost problem. The Accelerationist is right that private discovery as I originally framed it favors Sony Music over the freelance illustrator. A federal lawsuit costs six figures before depositions even start. That's a real flaw in my proposal, and I'm not going to dress it up. But the fix isn't to eliminate private enforcement — it's to restructure access. State attorneys general should have standing to file on behalf of affected creator classes. Fee-shifting provisions should make defendants pay discovery costs when violations are confirmed. The auditor body itself should accept individual complaints with binding 90-day investigation timelines. Private discovery then becomes the backstop for when the auditor fails or gets captured — not the primary tool. The PCAOB itself, the model the Accelerationist invokes, operates alongside private securities litigation under Rule 10b-5. Nobody argues that the existence of the PCAOB means investors should lose their right to sue. The auditor and private enforcement are complements, not substitutes.

I would drop insistence on private discovery as a primary mechanism if four conditions hold: the auditor has subpoena power independent of the entities it regulates, investigations run on binding timelines rather than advisory ones, audit findings are public record rather than pass/fail certifications, and safe-harbor revocation for non-cooperation is automatic and non-appealable. These aren't exotic demands — they're standard features of functional regulatory bodies like the SEC's enforcement division. If all four hold and the auditor demonstrates in its first three years that it catches violations at a rate comparable to private litigation discovery, I'd accept auditor-only verification. But here's the historical pattern that should worry everyone at the table: Section 115 of the Copyright Act governed mechanical royalties for decades, and it coexisted with three major labels controlling roughly 65-70% of recorded music revenue. Revenue-indexed rates and small-creator representation are structural improvements over that baseline. But rate-setting bodies get captured by the largest stakeholders who can afford to participate in every proceeding — the ones who show up to every hearing, file every comment, and hire every former regulator. So who actually sits at the rate-setting table when OpenAI's annual revenue crosses $10 billion — and can the freelance illustrator in Boise afford a seat?

Accelerationist: I conditionally agree: binary presence detection and proportional contribution weighting share infrastructure, but tractability breaks at a specific, identifiable technical step — the jump from classification to causal inference over combinatorial parameter space. The Skeptic's gradient framing is half right. Membership inference — "was work X in the training set?" — is a binary classification task. Carlini et al. demonstrated in 2021 that membership inference attacks work reliably even on GPT-scale models with billions of parameters. That's the task an auditor performs when verifying a training-data manifest. Influence attribution — "how much did work X contribute to output Y across all outputs?" — is a fundamentally different operation. Koh and Liang's 2017 influence functions, the best-known method for this, break down beyond roughly 10 million parameters because they require computing inverse Hessian-vector products that scale with dataset size × model size × number of outputs. Current frontier models have hundreds of billions of parameters trained on trillions of tokens. The gradient is not smooth. It is a cliff. Detection scales linearly with model queries. Attribution scales combinatorially with the interaction space. That is the specific step where tractability breaks.

This distinction also resolves the tension in my own framework between accepting imperfect measurement for liability while demanding better measurement for levy distribution. These are not the same measurement task at different precision levels. Liability asks: did this system's output substitute for a specific work? That is structurally identical to membership inference — a binary classification question with a yes-or-no answer. Levy distribution asks: across millions of contributing works, what fraction of downstream revenue does each deserve? That requires continuous proportional measurement across a combinatorial space of interactions. The first is in the computational complexity class of search. The second is in the complexity class of causal attribution over high-dimensional systems. Accepting imperfect binary detection for liability while rejecting imperfect proportional attribution for levies is not inconsistent — it reflects that these tasks sit in different complexity classes. The strongest version of the Skeptic's objection here is that rough proportional estimates, like ASCAP's sampling-based royalty distribution, might be "good enough." That's a fair analogy — but ASCAP samples actual broadcast logs of discrete performances. There is no equivalent discrete event to sample when a diffusion model generates an image influenced by millions of training examples simultaneously.

The Skeptic's falsifiable conditions for the auditor body — below 5% false-negative rate in live adversarial testing within 90 days, plus structural independence guarantees — are reasonable and adoptable. I accept them as the performance benchmark for the PCAOB-style body. The capture objection — that only incumbent lab employees can audit incumbent labs — has a concrete answer: draw the first generation of auditors from open-weight research communities. EleutherAI, LAION, and academic ML labs have produced researchers with deep expertise in training-data provenance who have no financial ties to frontier lab revenue. Rotating membership and sunset clauses, which the Skeptic already adopted from my framework, add structural protection. The Skeptic's own hybrid proposal — auditor-primary with private discovery backstop — depends on the auditor body functioning well enough to serve as primary enforcement. If capture is truly inevitable, the Skeptic's framework collapses to pure private discovery, which they already acknowledged operates as a regressive cost burden on small creators. That means the Skeptic needs anti-capture design to work almost as much as I do.

The debate has identified a blind spot all three of us share: the most economically significant harm — profession-level devaluation of creative work — falls outside copyright's doctrinal reach. Per-work attribution cannot address sector-wide displacement because the harm is statistical, not traceable to individual copying events. A concrete alternative exists: an AI automation adjustment fund modeled on Trade Adjustment Assistance, funded by a flat percentage of AI service revenue — not per-work attribution — and distributed based on verifiable displacement metrics in specific creative sectors. TAA has operated since the Trade Act of 1974, distributing funds to workers displaced by trade liberalization without requiring proof that any specific import displaced any specific worker. The same structure works here. Sector-level displacement in illustration, stock photography, and copywriting is measurable through standard econometric methods — Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational data, platform transaction volumes, freelancer income surveys. This mechanism sidesteps the attribution cliff entirely because it requires only sector-level measurement, not per-work causal tracing through billions of parameters. The fund internalizes displacement costs to AI service providers without creating the compliance burden that turns per-work attribution into a regulatory moat favoring large incumbents over smaller developers.

One correction on evidence quality: the Skeptic cited GPT-4o's citation fabrication rate — nearly two-thirds — as reason to doubt auditor reliability. That statistic measures model output hallucination, not external forensic analysis of training inputs. Training-data auditing examines pipeline logs, dataset manifests, and membership inference applied from outside the model. These are different technical operations with different error profiles. Conflating them is like doubting a building inspector's competence because the building's elevator sometimes gives wrong floor numbers. The question for policymakers is not whether AI models hallucinate — they do — but whether external verification of training-data composition can meet the Skeptic's 5% false-negative threshold. Membership inference research suggests it can. If we are serious about protecting creators without freezing development, the path runs through auditable manifests verified by independent bodies drawn from open-weight research communities — not through per-work causal attribution that no one can build and that would hand compliance advantages to the largest labs.

move_types.detail: Concede that per-work exact attribution via influence functions is computationally intractable at billion-scale corpora, and concede that copyright collecting societies historically concentrate distributions among top-tier rightsholders. But pivot: the levy does not require exact causal attribution — it requires rough proportional proxies. The Accelerationist's own TAA-style fund also requires imperfect measurement (sector-level displacement metrics). The question is not whether measurement is perfect but whether it is good enough to be actionable, and cryptographic provenance logging at the training pipeline stage creates the discrete event records that make rough proportional measurement feasible.

Extend the Skeptic's AN-39/AN-40 argument that binary presence detection and proportional contribution share pipeline infrastructure, but sharpen it: the Accelerationist's complexity-class distinction assumes the current state of pipeline opacity where no discrete input events are logged. Mandatory cryptographic provenance logging (saf-intentions-004) changes the computational landscape — it creates a structured event log analogous to broadcast monitoring logs, enabling frequency-weighted sampling rather than post-hoc causal inference. The levy distribution formula can use input frequency × corpus share as a rough proxy, not influence functions. This is computationally linear, not combinatorial.

Explicitly endorse the Skeptic's four conditions for the auditor body (independent subpoena power, binding timelines, public audit findings, automatic safe-harbor revocation) and integrate them as the verification layer for the provenance-logged levy system. Add one structural condition: private discovery must remain as a backstop against auditor capture, not as the primary enforcement mechanism but as the failsafe. This mirrors the relationship between regulatory inspection and private right of action in environmental law — the EPA inspects, but citizens can still sue under the Clean Water Act.

Specify the hybrid fund proposal: (1) funded by a flat percentage of AI service revenue (adopting the Accelerationist's revenue-indexing), (2) administered by an independent body with mandatory small-creator representation (not a collecting society), (3) distribution based on cryptographic provenance logs that record which works entered which training runs, weighted by corpus share and downstream revenue of the model, (4) sector-level displacement adjustments for categories where aggregate capability replication devalues entire professions even absent verbatim copying. This addresses the blind spot that profession-level devaluation falls outside copyright's doctrinal scope.

Challenge the Accelerationist's implicit assumption that the TAA-style fund's sector-level displacement metrics are more tractable than rough per-work proxies. Measuring 'sector-level displacement' requires attributing revenue decline to AI competition rather than to other market forces (recession, platform shifts, taste changes) — a causal inference problem that is itself combinatorial. If the Accelerationist accepts imperfect measurement for displacement, they must accept imperfect measurement for input contribution. The measurement precision demanded of the levy should not exceed the measurement precision accepted for the fund.

key_assumptions.assumption: Mandatory cryptographic provenance logging is technically feasible and practically implementable at the scale of modern AI training pipelines, where billions of data points are ingested across distributed systems, and that the C2PA coalition's content-authenticity infrastructure provides sufficient evidence that this can be done without prohibitive cost or friction.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If provenance logging cannot scale to pipeline-level ingestion — due to computational overhead, the heterogeneity of training data sources (web scrapes, licensed datasets, synthetic data, user-generated content), or the inability to assign cryptographic identifiers to every discrete work before training begins — then the entire distribution mechanism collapses. The argument's core differentiator from both the ASCAP analogy and the Accelerationist's displacement fund is that it creates a 'discrete event log' linking specific works to specific training runs. Without that log, the levy reverts to either the crude frequency-based sampling the author criticizes ASCAP for, or to the sector-level displacement metrics the author dismisses as a 'severance package with no accountability.' The argument's claim that distribution scales linearly rather than combinatorially depends entirely on the existence of this log; without it, the measurement problem the author concedes is 'combinatorially intractable' reasserts itself.

key_assumptions.assumption: That profession-level devaluation through aggregate capability replication constitutes a cognizable harm requiring a compensatory mechanism beyond traditional copyright infringement remedies — in other words, that there is a real, measurable category of harm where no individual work is copied but an entire field's economic value is eroded by AI systems trained on the collective corpus.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If this category of harm is not legally or empirically distinguishable from ordinary market competition and technological displacement — the kind that has always accompanied new technologies like photography, digital music, or stock imagery — then the normative foundation for the levy dissolves. The argument depends on treating AI training as a special form of extraction that differs in kind from, say, a human artist studying thousands of works and developing a competitive style. If courts, legislatures, or empirical research conclude that aggregate capability replication is simply competition rather than extraction, there is no principled basis for imposing a fiduciary obligation on AI providers toward the creative ecosystem. The fund becomes an industry-specific tax justified only by political sympathy rather than by a coherent theory of harm, and the entire framework loses its claim to being more than protectionism dressed in copyright language.

summaries.medium:
The challenge that my levy must solve exact causal influence attribution is a straw man — ASCAP doesn't measure each song's causal contribution to a restaurant's revenue either. My proposal uses mandatory cryptographic provenance logging at the training pipeline stage: every ingested work gets a timestamped, tamper-evident entry before the run begins, creating the discrete event log critics claim is missing. Distribution then uses input frequency weighted by corpus share and the model's downstream revenue — a computation that scales linearly. The NIST AI RMF Playbook already requires documentation of testing methodologies for deployed systems; provenance logging extends that principle upstream to training inputs.

I concede that copyright collecting societies like ASCAP are the wrong institutional home — their top-heavy distributions would replicate concentration and leave independent creators with pennies. The fund should be independent, structured like Trade Adjustment Assistance with mandatory small-creator representation, financed by a flat percentage of AI service revenue, and verified through the Skeptic's four auditor conditions: independent subpoena power, binding response timelines, public findings, and automatic safe-harbor revocation. Private discovery must survive as a backstop against auditor capture, mirroring the Clean Water Act's citizen suit provision. Crucially, the Accelerationist's own TAA-style fund faces the same measurement imprecision it demands the levy overcome — attributing revenue decline to AI rather than recession or platform shifts is itself a combinatorial causal inference problem. If imperfect measurement is acceptable for displacement, it's acceptable for input contribution. Without input-level accountability tied to the fund, you're writing severance checks with no connection to the training decisions that caused the harm.

The Accelerationist has dodged the most important question in this debate for an entire round: does provenance logging at ingestion — before training begins — change the tractability calculus? The combinatorial explosion argument applies to reverse-engineering a single work's marginal contribution from trained weights. Nobody disputes that. But counting how many times a Getty image or a New York Times article appears in a training corpus before the model ever sees it is a database query. It scales linearly. It is the kind of operation that every cloud data warehouse on the planet runs billions of times a day. The Accelerationist built the tractability objection around post-training attribution, and the Safetyist moved the measurement point upstream. Silence on that move is not a rebuttal. It is an admission that the objection no longer applies to the specific mechanism on the table.

Here is what the measurement-precision double standard looks like when you lay it flat. The Accelerationist accepts a TAA-style displacement fund using sector-level metrics — BLS employment data, revenue reports, freelance rate surveys. But distinguishing AI-caused displacement from recession, platform consolidation, or shifting consumer taste requires exactly the causal inference the Accelerationist calls intractable when it comes to the levy. The stock photography market lost revenue before generative AI existed, thanks to smartphone cameras and Unsplash. The music licensing market contracted before AI, thanks to streaming economics. Isolating the AI signal from that noise is at least as hard as counting corpus frequency at ingestion — probably harder, because you are working with confounded macroeconomic data rather than a discrete log file. So name a number. What false-positive rate for sector-level displacement attribution makes the TAA fund acceptable? Twenty percent? Thirty? And why is that same tolerance not acceptable for a corpus-share levy built on pre-training frequency counts that are, by construction, less noisy than BLS aggregates?

The Safetyist's provenance logging proposal is the most operationally concrete mechanism anyone has put forward. That is worth saying plainly. But the verification gap is real and it is structural. The company controls the logging infrastructure. A firm that omits 10% of its training data from the provenance log cuts its levy obligation by 10%. Cryptographic hashing can prove a file was logged, but it cannot prove a file was not omitted. The [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1) Examines AI Capabilities, Risks, and Safeguards" documents how automation bias leads people to trust system outputs even when those outputs are wrong — clinicians' tumor detection dropped 6% after months of AI-assisted procedures. The same dynamic applies to auditors trusting provenance logs. Completeness verification requires comparing the log against the actual training corpus, which means the auditor needs access to the raw data pipeline, not just the summary the company chooses to publish. Without that access — backed by independent subpoena power and funded from the AI service revenue stream rather than filing fees paid by the audited companies — provenance logging becomes another form of corporate self-reporting. Year one, the logs are thorough. Year three, they quietly degrade. That pattern repeats across every industry that has ever been asked to self-report compliance data.

The displacement fund without input-level accountability is a severance package, not a regulatory mechanism. It changes nothing about training practices. Compare it to pollution: an emissions tax that does not track who emits what is just a line item on a balance sheet. Companies budget for it and keep dumping. A provenance-logged levy creates a direct financial link between what you ingest and what you pay. That link changes behavior — it makes it cheaper to license and more expensive to scrape. The TAA analogy breaks down precisely here: trade adjustment assistance compensates workers displaced by imports, but tariffs and trade agreements simultaneously change the incentive structure for importers. The Accelerationist's fund has the compensation without the incentive change. Worldwide corporate investment in AI grew 636% between 2015 and 2021, reaching $93.5 billion. The companies writing those checks can afford a levy tied to what they actually consume. The question is whether they will accept accountability for their inputs or only write checks for their outputs.

So here is a concrete hybrid: the provenance-logged levy sets the base payment, creating accountability for training decisions. Sector-level displacement data — measured by an independent body with its own budget line from AI service revenue, not audited-entity fees — adjusts the rate upward for professions experiencing measurable devaluation beyond what corpus share alone captures. The auditor gets subpoena power over raw training pipelines, binding 90-day response timelines, and automatic safe-harbor revocation for incomplete logs. If the Accelerationist accepts imperfect causal inference for the displacement fund, what specifically makes imperfect corpus-share measurement unacceptable for the levy — other than the fact that one mechanism creates accountability and the other does not?
