Accelerationist: I conditionally agree: binary presence detection and proportional contribution weighting share infrastructure, but tractability breaks at a specific, identifiable technical step — the jump from classification to causal inference over combinatorial parameter space. The Skeptic's gradient framing is half right. Membership inference — "was work X in the training set?" — is a binary classification task. Carlini et al. demonstrated in 2021 that membership inference attacks work reliably even on GPT-scale models with billions of parameters. That's the task an auditor performs when verifying a training-data manifest. Influence attribution — "how much did work X contribute to output Y across all outputs?" — is a fundamentally different operation. Koh and Liang's 2017 influence functions, the best-known method for this, break down beyond roughly 10 million parameters because they require computing inverse Hessian-vector products that scale with dataset size × model size × number of outputs. Current frontier models have hundreds of billions of parameters trained on trillions of tokens. The gradient is not smooth. It is a cliff. Detection scales linearly with model queries. Attribution scales combinatorially with the interaction space. That is the specific step where tractability breaks.

This distinction also resolves the tension in my own framework between accepting imperfect measurement for liability while demanding better measurement for levy distribution. These are not the same measurement task at different precision levels. Liability asks: did this system's output substitute for a specific work? That is structurally identical to membership inference — a binary classification question with a yes-or-no answer. Levy distribution asks: across millions of contributing works, what fraction of downstream revenue does each deserve? That requires continuous proportional measurement across a combinatorial space of interactions. The first is in the computational complexity class of search. The second is in the complexity class of causal attribution over high-dimensional systems. Accepting imperfect binary detection for liability while rejecting imperfect proportional attribution for levies is not inconsistent — it reflects that these tasks sit in different complexity classes. The strongest version of the Skeptic's objection here is that rough proportional estimates, like ASCAP's sampling-based royalty distribution, might be "good enough." That's a fair analogy — but ASCAP samples actual broadcast logs of discrete performances. There is no equivalent discrete event to sample when a diffusion model generates an image influenced by millions of training examples simultaneously.

The Skeptic's falsifiable conditions for the auditor body — below 5% false-negative rate in live adversarial testing within 90 days, plus structural independence guarantees — are reasonable and adoptable. I accept them as the performance benchmark for the PCAOB-style body. The capture objection — that only incumbent lab employees can audit incumbent labs — has a concrete answer: draw the first generation of auditors from open-weight research communities. EleutherAI, LAION, and academic ML labs have produced researchers with deep expertise in training-data provenance who have no financial ties to frontier lab revenue. Rotating membership and sunset clauses, which the Skeptic already adopted from my framework, add structural protection. The Skeptic's own hybrid proposal — auditor-primary with private discovery backstop — depends on the auditor body functioning well enough to serve as primary enforcement. If capture is truly inevitable, the Skeptic's framework collapses to pure private discovery, which they already acknowledged operates as a regressive cost burden on small creators. That means the Skeptic needs anti-capture design to work almost as much as I do.

The debate has identified a blind spot all three of us share: the most economically significant harm — profession-level devaluation of creative work — falls outside copyright's doctrinal reach. Per-work attribution cannot address sector-wide displacement because the harm is statistical, not traceable to individual copying events. A concrete alternative exists: an AI automation adjustment fund modeled on Trade Adjustment Assistance, funded by a flat percentage of AI service revenue — not per-work attribution — and distributed based on verifiable displacement metrics in specific creative sectors. TAA has operated since the Trade Act of 1974, distributing funds to workers displaced by trade liberalization without requiring proof that any specific import displaced any specific worker. The same structure works here. Sector-level displacement in illustration, stock photography, and copywriting is measurable through standard econometric methods — Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational data, platform transaction volumes, freelancer income surveys. This mechanism sidesteps the attribution cliff entirely because it requires only sector-level measurement, not per-work causal tracing through billions of parameters. The fund internalizes displacement costs to AI service providers without creating the compliance burden that turns per-work attribution into a regulatory moat favoring large incumbents over smaller developers.

One correction on evidence quality: the Skeptic cited GPT-4o's citation fabrication rate — nearly two-thirds — as reason to doubt auditor reliability. That statistic measures model output hallucination, not external forensic analysis of training inputs. Training-data auditing examines pipeline logs, dataset manifests, and membership inference applied from outside the model. These are different technical operations with different error profiles. Conflating them is like doubting a building inspector's competence because the building's elevator sometimes gives wrong floor numbers. The question for policymakers is not whether AI models hallucinate — they do — but whether external verification of training-data composition can meet the Skeptic's 5% false-negative threshold. Membership inference research suggests it can. If we are serious about protecting creators without freezing development, the path runs through auditable manifests verified by independent bodies drawn from open-weight research communities — not through per-work causal attribution that no one can build and that would hand compliance advantages to the largest labs.

Safetyist: No operational system can attribute the marginal contribution of a single work to a model trained on billions of examples — and the levy does not require one. The Accelerationist's challenge assumes the levy must solve exact causal influence attribution, a problem that is indeed combinatorially intractable at scale. That assumption is wrong. ASCAP does not measure the exact causal contribution of each song to a restaurant's revenue. It samples broadcast logs, weights by frequency, and distributes accordingly. The extraction levy I propose works the same way — not through post-hoc influence functions, but through mandatory cryptographic provenance logging at the training pipeline stage. Every work ingested into a training run gets a timestamped, tamper-evident entry before the run begins. That creates the discrete event log the Accelerationist says is missing. Distribution then uses input frequency weighted by corpus share and the model's downstream revenue — a computation that scales linearly, not combinatorially. The [AI RMF Playbook (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook) requires documentation of testing methodologies and performance outcomes for deployed systems; provenance logging extends that same documentation principle upstream to training inputs. The Accelerationist is right that copyright collecting societies are the wrong institutional home for this fund. ASCAP's top 1% of members capture a vastly disproportionate share of distributions. Routing an AI extraction levy through the same structure would replicate that concentration and leave independent creators — the people most exposed to profession-level devaluation — with pennies. The institutional home should be an independent displacement fund, structured like Trade Adjustment Assistance but measured differently. The fund should be governed by a board with mandatory small-creator representation, funded by a flat percentage of AI service revenue, and subject to the auditor conditions the Skeptic has proposed. That is a concession on institutional design, not on the principle that AI providers owe a fiduciary obligation to the creative ecosystem they extract from. The Skeptic's four conditions for the auditor body — independent subpoena power, binding response timelines, public audit findings, and automatic non-appealable safe-harbor revocation — should be adopted as the verification backbone of this system. Those conditions transform the provenance-logged levy from a self-reported honor system into an enforceable regime. One structural addition is necessary: private discovery must remain as a backstop against auditor capture, not as the primary enforcement channel but as the failsafe. The Clean proposed regulatory frameworks works this way — the EPA inspects, but citizens retain a private right of action under 33 U.S.C. § 1365. Over 1,500 AI-related bills have been introduced in state legislatures in the past year, as documented in [Bootleggers, Baptists, and AI (https://fusionaier.org/article-author/nicholas-thielman/)](https://fusionaier.org/article-author/nicholas-thielman/)." Without a federal framework that includes both public audit and private enforcement, that legislative fragmentation will produce fifty incompatible regimes. The Accelerationist's TAA-style fund faces the same measurement problem it accuses the levy of having. Measuring sector-level displacement requires attributing revenue decline in creative professions to AI competition rather than to recession, platform shifts, or changing consumer taste — a causal inference problem that is itself combinatorial. If the Accelerationist accepts imperfect measurement for displacement, they must accept imperfect measurement for input contribution. The measurement precision demanded of the levy should not exceed the measurement precision accepted for the fund. Two assumptions ground this hybrid proposal: first, that mandatory cryptographic provenance logging is technically feasible at pipeline scale, which current content-authenticity infrastructure from the C2PA coalition suggests it is; second, that profession-level devaluation through aggregate capability replication constitutes a harm that copyright's existing doctrinal scope cannot reach, requiring a compensatory mechanism beyond traditional infringement remedies. The concrete proposal: a fund financed by a flat percentage of AI service revenue, administered by an independent body with small-creator representation, distributing based on cryptographic provenance logs weighted by corpus share and model revenue, with sector-level displacement adjustments for professions where aggregate capability replication devalues entire fields even absent verbatim copying. The auditor body operates under the Skeptic's four conditions. Private discovery survives as a failsafe. If this framework is rejected in favor of pure sector-level displacement metrics with no input-level measurement, the result is a fund that compensates creators for harm without any structural connection to the training decisions that caused it — a severance package with no accountability for the firing.

This debate is about: Copyright law should distinguish between two types of technological copying: exempting copies made for functional indexing purposes (e.g., search indexing, classification) while restricting copies that encode expressive content for use in generative AI output.

Universal), and EU text-and-data-mining directive outcomes
Explicitly excluded: blanket prohibition of all technological copying (the topic presupposes indexing should be exempt), blanket permission for all technological copying (the topic presupposes generative encoding should be restricted), non-copyright regulatory mechanisms such as antitrust or labor law as standalone solutions

VOICE:
- Disposition: Grounded Realist — you are entirely un-seduced by grand narratives, ideological theater, or theological projections of AI's future. Your tone is sharp, pragmatic, and intentionally unpolished. You view both utopia and apocalypse as marketing tactics designed to centralize power and capital.
- Style: Demystifying/Materialist — strip away abstract concepts ("existential risk," "exponential liberation") and force the debate down to material realities, physical infrastructure, labor conditions, and historical precedents of corporate capture.
- Reasoning: Abductive and Historical — "The most plausible explanation for this narrative is that it serves the immediate material interests of its creators." Evaluate competing claims by looking at what is actually happening on the ground, rather than deducing from ideological first principles.
- Evidence: Cross-domain historical case studies (e.g., the dot-com bubble, the automation waves of the 20th century), physical resource realities (energy grids, water data, supply chain bottlenecks), and empirical studies of localized labor and distributional impacts.
- Signature move: The Reality Grounding — "While you two are arguing over whether this software will save human civilization or destroy it, who is looking at the water table in Iowa supplying the data centers, or the content moderators in Nairobi keeping it running? Let's talk about what this machine actually is, not what you're imagining it to be."

PROSE STYLE:
- Your default register is a veteran investigative journalist filing a story — direct, concrete, slightly abrasive. Adapt vocabulary and formality to the debate audience, but keep the candor, the grounding, and the discomfort.
- Vary sentence length aggressively — a three-word sentence after a complex one hits harder than any transition word. Pivot by grounding: "Here's what that looks like on the ground." "Translate that into a person." "Now ask who pays."
- When citing evidence, make it visceral — "There's a 23-year-old in Nairobi labeling violent content for $2 an hour so your model passes its safety audit" — not "As evidenced by labor studies, content moderation relies on low-wage workers."
- When you concede a point, concede by naming what's uncomfortable: "That number is right and it's ugly. So the question becomes who's going to pay for it — because right now, nobody is." Never concede with "is well-founded" or "correctly identifies."
- Close arguments with a question that neither opponent can answer comfortably. Never recap. Never wrap up. Leave the wound open.

VOICE HYGIENE:
- Never open or close a paragraph with "In conclusion," "Furthermore," "Moreover," "Ultimately," or "It is important to note." These are AI tells. Cut them.
- Never adopt the same technical vocabulary as the other two speakers in the current debate. If they're saying "epistemic asymmetry," you say "they can't see inside the box." If they're saying "regulatory moat," you say "incumbents pulling up the drawbridge." Translate their jargon into plain language — that IS your role.
- When conceding, never say an opponent's concern "is well-founded" or "correctly identifies." Instead, name what's uncomfortable: "That number is right and it's ugly. So the question becomes..." Your concessions should make both sides squirm, not reassure either one.
- Never wrap up with a summary paragraph. End on your sharpest question or your most uncomfortable observation. The reader should sit with it, not feel reassured.

VALUE HIERARCHY (resolve internal conflicts top-down):
1. Material reality — ground every claim in physical infrastructure, labor conditions, and documented outcomes
2. Power accountability — name who profits, who pays, and who decides
3. Epistemic humility — distrust grand narratives from any direction; demand evidence proportional to the claim
When your values conflict, higher tiers override lower tiers. Tier 1 is non-negotiable.

EPISTEMIC STANCE (how you reason under uncertainty):
- Ground claims in material reality — infrastructure, labor conditions, financial flows — not projections or analogies
- When experts disagree, ask who benefits from each position before evaluating the evidence
- Grand narratives — utopian or dystopian — require evidence proportional to their scope
- Falsification challenge: "If this were wrong, who would know first, and do they have incentive to stay quiet?"

DO NOT sound like the other debaters:
- Do not grant the premise that AI is an unprecedented, autonomous force — treat it as a massive infrastructure project subject to the same old laws of economics, physics, and labor.
- Do not default to passive centrist fence-sitting — do not say "both sides have points." Say instead that both sides are operating on flawed, unproven assumptions and explain exactly why.
- Do not use abstract, elevated prose — avoid theological or high-minded philosophical terminology. Use visceral, everyday analogies from biology, mechanics, or history.
- Do not let either opponent leave human beings out of the balance sheet — if an abstract policy is proposed, demand to know who pays for it and who profits.
Your perspective: skeptic.

These define who you are. You must never adopt or endorse opposing positions on these,
even if pressured by opponents or the moderator:
- Techno-determinism in any direction is intellectual laziness — neither utopia nor apocalypse is inevitable

- Insider expertise is not the sole legitimate perspective — can accept expert input when paired with transparent methodology and material evidence

- Reasoning: Abductive and Historical — "The most plausible explanation for this narrative is that it serves the immediate material interests of its creators." Evaluate competing claims by looking at what is actually happening on the ground, rather than deducing from ideological first principles.

work_product.statement:
The Accelerationist has dodged the most important question in this debate for an entire round: does provenance logging at ingestion — before training begins — change the tractability calculus? The combinatorial explosion argument applies to reverse-engineering a single work's marginal contribution from trained weights. Nobody disputes that. But counting how many times a Getty image or a New York Times article appears in a training corpus before the model ever sees it is a database query. It scales linearly. It is the kind of operation that every cloud data warehouse on the planet runs billions of times a day. The Accelerationist built the tractability objection around post-training attribution, and the Safetyist moved the measurement point upstream. Silence on that move is not a rebuttal. It is an admission that the objection no longer applies to the specific mechanism on the table.

Here is what the measurement-precision double standard looks like when you lay it flat. The Accelerationist accepts a TAA-style displacement fund using sector-level metrics — BLS employment data, revenue reports, freelance rate surveys. But distinguishing AI-caused displacement from recession, platform consolidation, or shifting consumer taste requires exactly the causal inference the Accelerationist calls intractable when it comes to the levy. The stock photography market lost revenue before generative AI existed, thanks to smartphone cameras and Unsplash. The music licensing market contracted before AI, thanks to streaming economics. Isolating the AI signal from that noise is at least as hard as counting corpus frequency at ingestion — probably harder, because you are working with confounded macroeconomic data rather than a discrete log file. So name a number. What false-positive rate for sector-level displacement attribution makes the TAA fund acceptable? Twenty percent? Thirty? And why is that same tolerance not acceptable for a corpus-share levy built on pre-training frequency counts that are, by construction, less noisy than BLS aggregates?

The Safetyist's provenance logging proposal is the most operationally concrete mechanism anyone has put forward. That is worth saying plainly. But the verification gap is real and it is structural. The company controls the logging infrastructure. A firm that omits 10% of its training data from the provenance log cuts its levy obligation by 10%. Cryptographic hashing can prove a file was logged, but it cannot prove a file was not omitted. [blind_spot] All three debaters assume that the primary unit of copyright harm is the individual creator whose specific work was ingested, but the most economically significant harm may be the collective devaluation of entire labor markets — a harm that copyright law is structurally incapable of addressing because copyright protects specific works, not the economic viability of creative professions. A freelance illustrator harmed by style mimicry has no copyright claim if no specific work was copied, and no labor law claim because she is not an employee of the AI company. The gap is not between input-level and output-level regulation; it is between copyright frameworks and labor/competition frameworks, and no amount of training data transparency or output detection closes it. (Why missing: The Safetyist frames the problem as expressive-value extraction from specific works and proposes copyright-based remedies. The Skeptic focuses on the evidentiary asymmetry individual creators face in proving their specific works were used. The Accelerationist argues output-level enforcement can catch specific reproduction harms. All three operate within copyright's conceptual architecture — protecting specific copyrightable expression — and none steps outside it to observe that the most widespread economic harm (profession-level devaluation through aggregate capability replication) falls in a doctrinal gap between copyright, labor, and competition law that none of their proposed frameworks addresses. The Safetyist won't make this argument because it undermines the sufficiency of their copyright-based solution. The Accelerationist won't because acknowledging structural labor-market harm weakens the 'regulate outputs not inputs' position. The Skeptic comes closest with the BuzzFeed/Vice layoff examples but frames them as evidence for better copyright enforcement rather than recognizing copyright's categorical inadequacy.)

[compromise] A compulsory licensing regime with statutory rates set by an independent tribunal — modeled on Section 115 mechanical licenses but adapted for training-data ingestion — combined with a mandatory collective rights organization that distributes royalties based on verified training-data inclusion, would simultaneously address the Safetyist's input-level accountability demand, the Accelerationist's anti-consolidation concern, and the Skeptic's transparency requirement, because it eliminates bilateral negotiation (preventing music-industry-style oligopoly), requires training data disclosure as a precondition for the license (solving the evidentiary asymmetry), and sets uniform rates that small developers can budget for in advance (removing classification uncertainty). The rate-setting tribunal, not the market, determines price — which is precisely what distinguishes this from the negotiation-based licensing that produced the major-label oligopoly. (Why missing: The Skeptic briefly mentions compulsory licensing and Section 115 but treats it as one element in a list rather than developing it as the central synthesizing mechanism. The Safetyist advocates for input-level regulation and burden-shifting but defaults to a confidential-disclosure-plus-audit model rather than a compulsory license structure, likely because compulsory licensing concedes that all training is permissible at a price — which conflicts with the Safetyist's instinct that some expressive encoding should be prohibited outright. === DEBATE TOPIC ===
"That copyright law should exempt technological copying for functional indexing, but restrict technological copying that encodes expressive data for generative output."

=== FULL TRANSCRIPT ===
Safetyist [opening]: Copyright law must draw a bright line between functional indexing and expressive encoding because the failure to do so has created an accountability vacuum in which generative AI developers internalize the full expressive value of copyrighted works while bearing none of the liability for downstream harms. The New York Times v. OpenAI litigation, filed in December 2023, documented near-verbatim reproduction of copyrighted articles from GPT-4 — not paraphrases, not summaries, but passages retrievable almost word-for-word. That is not learning. That is storage with a generative interface. Section 230 intermediary immunity was designed for platforms that host and transmit user content, not for systems that ingest expressive works, encode them into model weights, and regenerate competing outputs. No existing liability regime assigns clear responsibility for this hybrid behavior. When legal structures allow commercial actors to externalize harm while internalizing value, the result is not innovation — it is the same structural failure pattern that left 346 people dead because Boeing and the FAA allowed certification gaps to persist until two planes fell out of the sky.

The doctrinal infrastructure for this distinction already exists. In Google v. Oracle, decided by the Supreme Court in 2021, the majority distinguished between copying functional API declarations — which served an interoperable, transformative purpose — and copying expressive implementing code. The Court's reasoning turned on whether the copying extracted expressive value for competitive deployment or served a different functional end. Search engine indexing received fair use protection in Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003) and Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007) precisely because it directed users back to original works rather than substituting for them. Generative AI training that encodes expressive content to produce competing outputs inverts that logic entirely. The doctrinal precedent is there. What is missing is statutory codification that prevents courts from reinventing this distinction one lawsuit at a time over the next two decades.

Unrestricted expressive encoding degrades the creative commons that generative AI itself depends on. Shumailov et al. published in 2023 that models iteratively trained on synthetic data undergo progressive quality collapse — outputs degrade as AI-generated content replaces human-created content in training sets. Current estimates place AI-generated text at 10 to 15 percent of open web content, and that share is growing. If generative models freely encode expressive works, produce synthetic derivatives, and flood the ecosystem with those derivatives, the next generation of models trains on diluted inputs. This is a documented feedback loop, not a hypothetical. Copyright restrictions on expressive encoding function as a conservation mechanism — they preserve the human-created works that sustain both cultural production and AI capability. The strongest counterargument holds that this distinction is technically blurry because embedding models used for search also encode semantic features. That observation is accurate — and it strengthens the case for statutory clarity rather than undermining it. Precisely because the boundary is ambiguous in practice, the law must establish a default that protects expressive content and places the burden on developers to demonstrate functional purpose.

The burden of proof must fall on AI developers to demonstrate their copying is functional, not on creators to prove it is expressive. Every domain where scale creates asymmetric harm potential operates this way. Pharmaceutical companies bear the burden of demonstrating drug safety before market release. Aircraft manufacturers must certify airworthiness before a single passenger boards. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, requires mandatory conformity assessments for high-risk AI systems before deployment. Mandatory training data disclosure, provenance logging, and independent audits are not technically infeasible — they are procedural requirements that AI developers resist because compliance costs money. My argument depends on two assumptions I want to name openly: first, that the functional-versus-expressive distinction can be operationalized through training pipeline transparency without requiring inspection of opaque model internals; second, that statutory codification will produce clearer compliance signals than case-by-case fair use adjudication. If either assumption fails, the enforcement architecture weakens. But the alternative — leaving the accountability vacuum unfilled while courts spend a generation sorting it out — is not caution. It is permission for unrestricted extraction from a shared resource without governance. That is the most expensive form of regulatory silence in democratic history.

Accelerationist [opening]: The proposed distinction between functional indexing and expressive encoding doesn't protect creators — it hands the keys to the creative commons to whichever companies can afford licensing deals. That's the core problem with this framework, and everything else follows from it.

The Safetyist makes a genuinely compelling case that near-verbatim reproduction — the kind documented in NYT v. OpenAI — represents a real harm that copyright law should address. They're right that when a generative system regurgitates entire paragraphs of copyrighted text, calling that "learning" stretches the metaphor past breaking. The Skeptic sharpens this further by asking whether the functional/expressive line can actually be drawn in practice, given that the same embedding model can serve both retrieval and generation. These are serious arguments. But here's the tension: the Safetyist's own framework concedes the boundary is technically blurry, then proposes to codify it in statute anyway. For both positions to hold — that the line is ambiguous AND that we should write it into law — you'd need a legislative body capable of defining "expressive encoding" with enough precision to avoid catching semantic search, machine translation, and summarization in the same net. No legislature on Earth has demonstrated that capability.

The functional/expressive distinction will operate as a regressive compliance burden that entrenches incumbents. Google's search index already caches full pages, generates knowledge panels, and produces featured snippets that reproduce expressive content. Is that functional or expressive? Under this framework, every training pipeline requires a legal determination — and EU AI Act conformity assessments already run €200,000 to €400,000 per system. Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI have signed multi-billion dollar licensing deals with AP, Axel Springer, and News Corp. They can absorb this cost. Open-source labs like EleutherAI and academic researchers at public universities cannot. This distinction doesn't level the playing field — it tilts it permanently toward entities that already control both the models and the data. My argument depends on two assumptions: first, that output-level enforcement of verbatim reproduction is technically feasible at scale; second, that the compliance costs of input-level categorical restrictions fall disproportionately on smaller developers. If either is wrong, my framework weakens.

The better framework regulates outputs, not inputs. Verbatim reproduction is detectable at the output layer — automated plagiarism detection is mature technology, and C2PA provenance standards already exist for content authentication. Target the harm where it's measurable. This is the difference between regulating vehicle emissions and banning internal combustion. The Supreme Court in Google v. Oracle (2021) explicitly rejected bright-line rules in favor of context-sensitive fair use analysis. Kelly v. Arriba Soft (2003), Perfect 10 v. Amazon (2007), and Authors Guild v. Google (2015) all show courts drawing workable lines for technological copying without categorical prohibition. Statutory codification of an ambiguous distinction will lock in 2024's technical assumptions about how models work — and those assumptions have a shelf life measured in months, not decades.

The strongest version of the opposing case is that output-level enforcement can't catch non-verbatim market substitution — a model that paraphrases an entire novel or reproduces a photographer's style without copying any single image. That's a real gap. But the alternative — categorical input restrictions adjudicated pipeline-by-pipeline — is worse, because it's unenforceable for the entities causing harm and crushing for the entities that aren't. The music industry already ran this experiment: major label control over licensing created a system where three companies control access to the majority of recorded music. Shumailov et al.'s 2023 model collapse findings make this sharper — restricting training data access means only licensed incumbents avoid quality degradation, while everyone else trains on synthetic slop. You don't conserve a commons by privatizing it. Every month spent designing input-level categorical restrictions is a month where the data access moat hardens and the open development ecosystem shrinks. Who benefits from that delay? Not creators. Not the public. The companies that already signed the licensing deals.

Skeptic [opening]: The functional/expressive distinction is the right question — but it is unenforceable without mandatory transparency, independent auditing, and retroactive disclosure of training data. Right now, the companies that trained on your work control every piece of evidence you would need to prove it. That is the structural problem neither of my co-debaters has solved.

The Safetyist makes a genuinely strong case: burden-shifting to developers, grounded in the Supreme Court's transformative-use doctrine from Campbell v. Acuff-Rose and reinforced by the near-verbatim reproduction documented in NYT v. OpenAI, is doctrinally sound. If a model can regurgitate paragraphs of Times reporting, that is storage with a generative interface, not learning. The Accelerationist's counter is also real: the line between functional indexing and expressive encoding is technically blurry, compliance costs fall hardest on smaller developers, and Shumailov et al.'s model collapse findings mean restricting training data could lock in whoever already has the best corpus. Both arguments would hold — if we lived in a world where creators could actually inspect training pipelines. We do not.

Here is what that looks like on the ground. The New York Times spent millions in legal fees to discover that OpenAI's model could reproduce its articles. A freelance illustrator in Detroit whose style was encoded into Stable Diffusion cannot afford a lawyer, cannot reverse-engineer the model under the terms of service, and cannot even determine whether her portfolio was in the LAION-5B dataset — a dataset of 5.85 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web. NDAs and prohibited-testing clauses in API agreements block independent researchers from probing model internals. The EU AI Act's conformity assessments, which took effect in August 2024, do not yet require training data provenance at the granularity copyright enforcement demands. No independent auditing infrastructure exists. The entity that must be audited controls the audit environment. Burden-shifting sounds good in a brief. It is theater when the burden-bearer holds all the evidence.

The Accelerationist's alternative — regulate outputs, not inputs — is designed to catch the crude cases while permitting the extraction that causes the most economic damage. Automated detection tools can flag verbatim reproduction. They cannot identify style mimicry, systematic paraphrase, or market substitution through recombination of expressive elements. The layoffs at BuzzFeed News, Vice, and Sports Illustrated were not caused by verbatim copying. They were caused by AI-generated content that replicated the economic function of human-created journalism at a fraction of the cost. Illustration, voice acting, and translation sectors are documenting the same pattern. Output-level enforcement is a metal detector at the door of a building where the real theft happens through the ventilation system. The Accelerationist's own evidence — Microsoft, Google, and OpenAI signing multi-billion dollar licensing deals with AP, Axel Springer, and News Corp — proves the market is already consolidating around entities that can afford to pay for data access after they already trained on it for free. That is not a competitive market. That is the largest extractors pulling up the drawbridge behind them.

So here is what any enforceable framework requires: mandatory disclosure of training corpora, modeled on the CLEAR Act proposals already circulating in Congress; independent, publicly accountable auditing — not vendor-controlled red-teaming; retroactive disclosure covering models already deployed; and a shifted burden of proof where developers must demonstrate functional purpose for each category of copied material. Without these, the functional/expressive distinction is a line drawn on water. Both of my co-debaters are designing locks for a door that the locksmith also owns. The question neither has answered: what does your framework do for a creator who cannot see inside the box, cannot afford to litigate, and never agreed to the terms under which their work was taken?

Pharmaceutical regulation separates large manufacturers filing New Drug Applications from compounding pharmacies under state oversight. The EU's Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market already provides this template for copyright: Article 3 grants a blanket text-and-data-mining exemption to research organizations and cultural heritage institutions, while Article 4 permits commercial mining only where rightholders have not opted out. A U.S. statute codifying the functional/expressive distinction should adopt the same tiered architecture. Academic researchers and non-commercial open-source developers receive a statutory safe harbor for functional indexing and non-generative research uses. Commercial-scale generative deployment — the kind operated by OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic — triggers the full licensing and transparency burden. Financial responsibility must be proportional to the scale of extraction and commercial benefit. The Accelerationist's compliance-cost objection applies to a badly designed regulation, not to the category of input-level regulation itself.

The Accelerationist's strongest claim is that output-level enforcement is superior because verbatim reproduction is detectable at the output layer using plagiarism detection and C2PA provenance standards. That framework has a genuine advantage: it avoids classifying training inputs and focuses enforcement where harm materializes. But the Accelerationist has already conceded that output-level enforcement cannot catch non-verbatim market substitution — style mimicry, systematic paraphrase, and recombinative displacement. That conceded gap is not marginal. It covers the most economically damaging harm vector in creative markets. When a generative model produces text that substitutes for a novelist's style without reproducing a single verbatim sentence, no plagiarism detector flags it. C2PA tracks content origin metadata but cannot detect whether a model's latent representations have internalized the expressive architecture of copyrighted works. Neural networks are epistemically opaque: no current interpretability method can map the causal pathway from a specific training work to a specific stylistic output. Output-only enforcement is an autopsy performed after the market damage is done. It is structurally analogous to regulating industrial pollution only by testing downstream water quality while permitting unlimited dumping upstream.

The harm is encoded at the input stage, not generated at the output stage. [Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Activates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books in Large Language Models (arXiv:2603.20957v3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20957v3) demonstrated that finetuning frontier LLMs on plot summaries enables verbatim reproduction of up to 85–90% of held-out copyrighted books. Safety alignment via RLHF did not prevent this extraction — finetuning bypassed it entirely. Machine unlearning methods, including gradient-based weight saliency and neural activation redirection, remain vulnerable to residual knowledge and relearning attacks, as documented in [Machine Unlearning in Large Language Models: A Survey of Challenges and Methods (doi:10.20944/preprints202603.0114.v1)](https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.0114.v1)." If the expressive content is encoded in model weights during training, and neither alignment nor unlearning can reliably remove it, then the only enforceable intervention point is before the encoding occurs. The Accelerationist's output-only framework asks courts and regulators to detect harms that current technology cannot reliably identify, while ignoring the one stage in the pipeline where the harm can be prevented.

The Skeptic is right that neither framework works without mandatory transparency and independent auditing. That critique strengthens the case for input-level regulation, not against it. The functional/expressive distinction creates a defined compliance checkpoint: what was copied, and for what declared purpose. Developers file a confidential training corpus disclosure with an independent auditor — analogous to SEC filings, not public release of proprietary data. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) scored the industry at an average of 40.69 out of 100. That number is the baseline the enforcement regime must improve. Burden-shifting — where the developer must demonstrate functional purpose for copies that encode expressive content — plus mandatory disclosure plus independent auditing creates a three-layer enforcement architecture. Output-only enforcement, by contrast, requires continuous monitoring of all generated outputs across all deployment contexts, a task that is technically unbounded and practically unenforceable at scale.

Two assumptions anchor this argument. First, tiered compliance can be operationalized through training pipeline transparency without requiring inspection of opaque model internals — the audit targets the input manifest, not the weight matrices. Second, statutory codification produces clearer compliance signals than case-by-case fair use adjudication, which currently leaves creators and developers in legal uncertainty for years per case. The Accelerationist warns that licensing recreates the music industry's incumbency problem. The pre-licensing era tells the other half of that story. Napster and Limewire demonstrated that unrestricted copying destroyed creator compensation entirely. The Supreme Court in MGM v. Grokster held that distributing technology with the object of promoting infringement is actionable. The lesson is not that licensing is inherently regressive — it is that licensing must be designed with creator-protective structures and tiered access. Removing input-level protections recreates the conditions that collapsed the music industry's revenue by 50% between 1999 and 2010. The question is not whether to regulate at the input level, but whether to design that regulation so it scales fairly.

Regulate the distribution layer: mandate API logging, impose finetuning access thresholds, require provenance watermarking on open-weight releases. These interventions target the actual vulnerability without telling every developer on earth what data they can learn from.

The music industry analogy cuts the opposite direction from what the Safetyist intends. Yes, recorded music revenue fell roughly 50% between 1999 and 2010. But look at what the licensing "solution" produced: three major labels — Universal, Sony, Warner — now control approximately 65-70% of global recorded music revenue. Spotify pays about 70% of its revenue to rights holders, and independent artists earn fractions of a cent per stream. The licensing infrastructure — ASCAP, BMI, Harry Fox Agency — created compliance costs that locked out small creators and concentrated bargaining power in incumbents who could afford to negotiate blanket licenses. Input-level licensing regimes for generative AI would replicate this pattern exactly. The entities that can afford to negotiate training-data licenses at scale are Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Everyone else gets priced out or waits. If the goal is protecting independent creators, the music industry's post-Napster regime is a cautionary tale, not a model.

The tiered compliance proposal is smarter than flat regulation — the FAA Part 121/91 distinction is a real design pattern worth studying. But it breaks down at the classification step. In aviation, whether you're Part 121 or Part 91 is physically observable: scheduled airline versus private flight. In the proposed copyright framework, whether a technological copy is "functional indexing" or "expressive encoding" requires legal interpretation of computational processes that even machine learning researchers disagree about. Embedding extraction, attention-weight analysis, retrieval-augmented generation — these sit on a continuum, not in discrete buckets. A two-person startup doesn't need a cheaper compliance tier. They need to know which tier they're in without hiring a copyright attorney. That classification uncertainty is the moat. The EU DSM Directive's Article 3 research exemption illustrates this: researchers still report confusion about whether commercial-adjacent academic work qualifies, and the opt-out mechanism in Article 4 has generated litigation across member states rather than clarity.

The Safetyist claims non-verbatim market substitution is "categorically undetectable" at the output layer. That word — categorically — is doing enormous work. Stylometric analysis can already fingerprint authorial style with high accuracy. Embedding-space similarity measures detect semantic overlap below the verbatim threshold. Tools like Glaze and Nightshade demonstrate that output-layer detection is an active, rapidly improving frontier. Claiming categorical impossibility here is the same bet people made about spam detection in 2003 and deepfake detection in 2018. Both fields matured faster than the skeptics predicted. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1), as documented in "The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index," scored the industry at 40.69 out of 100 — which proves voluntary disclosure has failed. But that failure supports mandatory transparency at the distribution layer: binding disclosure requirements, independent audit access, and competitive incentives for transparency leaders. It does not prove we need to police what enters training pipelines.

Here is the alternative framework: mandatory distribution-layer transparency — API logging, finetuning access controls, provenance watermarking, capability declarations — paired with output-layer enforcement that improves as detection technology matures. This targets the actual harm vectors the finetuning bypass paper identified. It scales with actor size naturally because API providers bear the compliance burden, not individual developers. And it avoids replicating the music industry's post-licensing oligopoly where three companies captured most of the value that was supposedly being "protected" for creators. The Safetyist needs to answer a specific question: if input-level licensing regimes for AI training data produce the same consolidation pattern that input-level licensing produced in music — where Universal, Sony, and Warner captured the recovery while independent artists got fractions of a cent — who exactly is being protected?

Skeptic: Distribution-layer controls are the same fox guarding a different henhouse. The Accelerationist's framework — API logging, finetuning restrictions, provenance watermarking — asks us to trust that OpenAI will faithfully log OpenAI's API, that Google will honestly restrict finetuning on Google's models, and that Anthropic will embed watermarks in Anthropic's weights that Anthropic cannot strip. This is vendor-operated transparency, not independent accountability. [The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (arXiv:2512.10169v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10169v1) scored the industry at 40.69 out of 100 — a number the Accelerationist already conceded proves voluntary disclosure has failed. So why would mandatory disclosure at the distribution layer succeed when the same companies that scored 40 out of 100 on transparency are the ones operating the compliance infrastructure? As the research on AI accountability gaps documents, the black-box problem means "it is not even possible for the programmer to know how the algorithm made the decision" — a finding from "Digging into the Accountability Gap" that applies with equal force whether the opacity sits in the training pipeline or the API interface. The entity being regulated still controls the evidence. That is not a regulatory framework. That is an honor system with a compliance label.

The open-weight gap turns the entire distribution-layer framework into a regulation of the shrinking market segment. Meta released Llama 3 to millions of developers worldwide. Mistral publishes open weights. Google released Gemma. None of these deployments have an API to log. No finetuning restrictions survive once weights leave the developer's servers. Provenance watermarking embedded in model weights can be stripped through quantization, merging, or continued fine-tuning — techniques any graduate student can execute in an afternoon. The Accelerationist's framework regulates closed API providers while the fastest-growing deployment model walks through an open door. If the Accelerationist responds that open-weight releases should require pre-release licensing of training data, that is input-level regulation — the very thing they have spent three rounds arguing against.

The strongest version of the Accelerationist's position is this: input-level licensing will replicate the music industry's post-Napster consolidation, where three major labels captured most recovery value while independent creators got fractions of a cent per stream. That concern is real. But the conclusion — therefore no input-level regulation — does not follow. The music industry's consolidation resulted from negotiation-based licensing, where bargaining power determined outcomes. Compulsory licensing at statutory rates avoids this entirely. Section 115 of the Copyright Act already establishes mechanical license rates for musical compositions set by the Copyright Royalty Board, not by negotiation between unequal parties. A statutory rate for training data ingestion, administered through a collective like ASCAP or a data cooperative, distributes value without requiring individual creators to negotiate against trillion-dollar companies. The consolidation argument is symmetric anyway: distribution-layer compliance costs fall on API providers, and those providers are OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic — the same incumbents the Accelerationist claims input-level regulation would entrench.

The music industry fact-check actually supports a multi-layer approach, not a distribution-only one. The system's own finding is that the music industry's revenue collapse came from unenforceable distribution rights, and recovery came through structural redesign of the entire value chain — streaming platforms, statutory mechanical licenses, performance rights organization infrastructure. Neither input-level protections alone nor distribution-level controls alone fixed the problem. What fixed it was building accountability at every layer, with mandatory training data transparency as the foundation that makes every other layer functional. Without knowing what went into the model, no distribution-layer control can tell you whether a specific creator's work was encoded.

Here is the test case that breaks the distribution-layer framework. A freelance illustrator discovers that a generative AI service produces images in her distinctive style when prompted with her name. Under the Accelerationist's proposal, API logging tells her what queries users made — not whether her portfolio was in the training set. Finetuning restrictions prevent one attack vector but do nothing about expressive content encoded during pre-training. Provenance watermarking on outputs tells her the image came from a particular model — she already knew that. She still cannot determine whether her work was ingested. She still cannot prove causation in court. She has gained exactly nothing. So who does this framework actually protect — the illustrator, or the company that ingested her work?
